items.title: Bitcoin Stablecoins and the Freedom to Choose
items.text:
After attending bitcoin++ Berlin, payments edition, two talks have been stuck in my head.

Allen Farrington’s [The Fiat Payment Stack Returns (Part 2), The Sequel](https://btcpp.dev/berlin26#berlin26_fiat_bf4b) explored how complicated fiat payments are underneath the familiar experience of tapping a card.

Then Lightrider’s [It Worked on My Node](https://btcpp.dev/berlin26#berlin26_worked_c209) showed us real numbers from nadanada.me. Once they added credit cards, Monero, shitcoins, and stablecoins, Bitcoin payments became a minority. And lightning is now just 10% of their payments.

Cryptorefills’ checkout data tells a similar story: stablecoins overtook Bitcoin in 2021 and now account for roughly two thirds of completed purchases on its platform.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160195)

I recommend watching both when the recordings are published. Together, they left me with an uncomfortable thought: the payment system we want to replace is a mess, yet people still aren’t choosing ours. I think we should take that seriously.

Bitcoin is a miracle. We have scarce digital money that we can hold under our own keys, without a bank deciding whether we deserve access. Nobody gets to print more. That is extraordinary.

We have won something enormous: the ability to save outside the banking system. I remain very bullish. Bitcoin is volatile, but my bet over the long run is still up and to the right.

But we haven’t won everyday payments. And perhaps we’ve spent too much time treating those as the same problem.

You might be happy to hold bitcoin through volatility. But a merchant trying to pay wages and suppliers may not be. Accepting bitcoin and wanting to keep bitcoin are different decisions. Meanwhile, a customer’s card is familiar, costs nothing to the user, and works everywhere.

If they choose that, it's not because they are "dumb". They’re solving their problems.

If we believe in free markets, the market gets to disagree with us. We should be curious about what people want, and build something worth choosing.

There is plenty to improve. Visa and Mastercard payments involve issuers, acquirers, processors, networks, currency conversion, and reconciliation. Merchants pay for that machinery, and the fees hurt when margins are thin. International transfers can be worse: in the third quarter of 2025, sending a $200 remittance cost 6.36% on average globally. Almost $13 just to move $200.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160191)

Stablecoins give people something immediately useful: familiar money that can move over an open network. For someone with an unstable local currency, limited banking access, or customers abroad, a digital dollar can solve a real problem today. Just like Bitcoin, but with less volatility.

Yes, stablecoins are fiat squared. You inherit fiat’s problems and add an issuer who can fail, restrict redemption, or freeze your tokens. But people are comparing them with the bank accounts and payment services they actually have. We should do the same.

I’m also unconvinced that CBDCs are the inevitable future. Several early launches have struggled to attract meaningful use. Governments can launch a product; they can’t manufacture a reason to want it.

My bet is that stablecoins will become the dominant way money moves across the internet, eventually taking over much of what card networks do today. People may still tap cards. Visa and Mastercard may adapt and thrive. The interface can stay familiar while the money underneath changes.

I often see Paolo Ardoino depicted as evil in Bitcoin circles. I don't know if he is. But what matters is whether he is right about stablecoins. And he might be.

Which brings me to the part that excites me: those dollars could move over Lightning.

What's the best "house" for stablecoins? There are many blockchains available. And looks like Tron is winning. Then Ethereum, Solana, Binance, ... So it's not like their users appreciate security and decentralization the most. Running a full node for any of those requires expensive equipment. Apart from other issues like PoS and even shittier version of that that give control to a handful or operators. But they are cheap. Big blocks, coming out every few seconds.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160192)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160194)

But blockchains don't scale. So if the whole world population would be using stablecoins, none of those would be able to keep up. At least without becoming a centralized database which might be too much even for the most careless shitcoiners.

But we have already solved that! No blockchain will be ever capable of competing with a channel based payments network like lightning. In terms of throughput and fees. So maybe Lightning is the best "house" for stablecoins after all.

Payment channels let us make many payments without recording every one on a global ledger. Bitcoin provides the foundation, while payments happen across a network of channels. I think that is a powerful architecture for global payments.

With Taproot Assets, a dollar payment can be exchanged into bitcoin at one edge, routed through Lightning, and exchanged into the recipient’s asset at the other. The customer can spend dollars. The merchant can receive dollars. Bitcoin can connect them without either having to share our monetary convictions.

Somebody has to provide liquidity and make the exchanges worthwhile. But the architecture is real. Tether has announced plans to bring USDt to Bitcoin and Lightning through Taproot Assets. I think we should be paying attention.

And honestly once on Lightning, the interoperability of Taproot assets with real bitcoin makes it too easy to switch. So that's another win there. Would be way easier to go from stablecoins to bitcoin than from fiat in a bank account to bitcoin, which is the current baseline.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160193)

The difficult part will be making it pleasant to use.

Self-custodial Lightning still involves channels, liquidity, backups, and recovery. We can improve that experience, but wishing everyone would run their own infrastructure won’t make it happen.

Some people will choose a provider. Others will want their own keys. Tools like Cashu offer another useful possibility: private ecash, backed by a mint the user trusts. That involves custody, but can offer privacy that an ordinary payment account doesn’t.

I can imagine wallets, mints, and payment companies connected through Lightning, competing to serve people who want to spend different kinds of money. What matters is whether users can move between them, withdraw their funds, recover from mistakes, and take more control when they want to.

Max Hillebrand’s *The Praxeology of Privacy* helped me think about this. I take from it an emphasis on practical progress toward autonomy. We don’t have to wait for everyone to adopt our ideal setup before helping them become freer.

Freedom comes before Bitcoin.

Bitcoin matters because of what it lets people do. If someone wants dollars for spending, I want to help them use dollars with lower costs, better privacy, and more choice. If they later want sovereign savings, Bitcoin should be within reach. The immediate benefit should be theirs, not our satisfaction at having converted another person.

I might be wrong about stablecoins winning, or Lightning becoming their best network. The honest way to find out is to listen, build, and compete.

Bitcoin has given people an extraordinary way to save. Now let’s give them better ways to spend, with useful wallets, private payments, and services they can leave as easily as they can join.

items.title: Lodging for Wayfaring Men Book Club #1: Farber's First Essay
items.text:
*Welcome to the first week of our book club reading *A Lodging for Wayfaring Men*! We're reading one chapter every two weeks, so we'll be discussing Chapter 1 next Saturday, but in between-weeks we are having a look at the essays in Appendix B. They are short and accessible.*

*You can find the book club reading schedule here:* https://stacker.news/items/1582413

---

# Farber's First Essay Discussion (full text of the essay available below)

Brutish, nasty, and short seems to have been an accurate description of human life until recently. About three hundred years ago (maybe longer), something changed:

> It is the great discovery of the modern era: the positive-sum game. It is the liberation of human energy to do its appropriate job. It is the operation of creation, using the only counter-entropic force we have: free human energy.

This, at least, is how Farber explains the difference between human civilization now and whatever club-swinging, animal-pelt-wearing past we came from. 

It's not obvious to me that trade -- this positive-sum game -- requires any particularly advanced sort of technology. Humans have had money and markets for thousands of years, but there wasn't progress in the sense of species-reshaping progress until the era of the industrial revolution. So what gives? Why would it take humans so long to come to the conclusion that trade is better than violence?

Farber says:

> It was only when a few freelance merchants began living according to their own minds and breaking away from the permissions of their rulers that things began to change.

He claims they discovered that freedom leads to creativity (and motivation, happiness, and the accumulation of wealth) but doesn't go into the question of why those freelance merchants figured it out when all the rest of humanity seemed to not get it -- or whether there was something standing in the way of them acting on the realization that freedom = prosperity.

There's no question in my mind that most of *recorded* human history consists of people beating on each other with sticks and swords and generally relying on violence far more than trade. It is possible that trade just faded into the background because it's not as sexy -- Homer didn't write epic poems about the mercantile abilities of Rufus the Greek. Perhaps there actually was quite a lot of freedom and trade going on all the time, but I rather suspect that there is something about humans that tends towards violence.

Later, Farber draws a link between the lack of freedom and the brutish animal life:

> They who do not play the positive-sum game instinctively fall back into being motivated by envy. Ultimately, they find reasons to feel that “there are only so many pieces of the pie.” This is the seed of destruction.
>
> The next thing they say is “if you have a bigger piece of the pie, then someone else has to have less.” That is a zero-sum game – the idea that nothing is really created, just moved from one hand to another. Not only is it false, but it is also the credo of every envious looter who speaks of ‘fairness’ and ‘equal distribution of wealth,’ but who secretly hopes to get a share of wealth held by others.

As much as this great era of human creativity in which we now live was the result of an expansion of human freedom, there is no guarantee that such freedom will be preserved. When I look around me, most of what I see are organized efforts at restricting human freedom (aka governments) growing more powerful.

So the question I'm interested in is what happened to restrain the violence? that allowed the "freelance merchants" to break away and live "according to their own minds" and how can we continue to make it clear to people that restrictions on human freedom only lead to violence?

---

# Farber's First Essay 

It began with Arab traders and the merchants of Venice. They really didn’t know what they were building or how it would work. They merely struggled for the betterment of themselves and their families.

It began to break out when the deep superstition of the middle ages cracked open under the strain of new philosophies and religious ideas. 

It found room to grow wherever new and wild vistas were found. It found fresh growth with each discovery of far-off new lands. It found a home everywhere the old order was broken up and fresh starts were being made. It took a firm root in America and flourished there for over a hundred years.

Never again, where history is recorded, will there be any question as to whether or not it works.

“It,” is the great discovery of the modern era: the positive-sum game. It is the liberation of human energy to do its appropriate job. It is the operation of creation, using the only counter-entropic force we have: free human energy.

You can see it work everywhere from the research lab, to the front office, to the construction site. It is what drives the entrepreneur to develop and produce a new product or service, and it is what gives the construction worker pride when his skill overcomes a difficult problem, making a way for his blueprints to become a functional structure. Why is the construction worker proud, and why does the entrepreneur exult? Because they have done the one thing that all humans have the impulse to do – to create something good that would not have been otherwise. Human energy is the great creative force in the world. Without it, things tend to entropy. (As the second law of thermodynamics states, “closed systems tend to entropy.”) Without active and creative human energy, everything goes back to an animal level of existence.

This human energy does not function by obedience and compulsion – itcannot, no matter how many rulers wish it were otherwise. Look at the command economies of the dead socialist world. Within several decades their occupants were reduced to an animal existence. Look at the millennia when constrained people lived at the pleasure of their Kings, seeking permissions from their rulers to live and work. They continually starved and died. It was only when a few freelance merchants began living according to their own minds and breaking away from the permissions of their rulers that things began to change. 

When human energy is free to move, creativity goes wild; as do motivation, happiness, and the accumulation of wealth. When it is restrained, the descent to animal existence takes over again. 

The discovery of this fact is what differentiates us from the middle ages, and not much else. Do you think the people who lived in those dark times were inherently less intelligent than we are? They were not! You and I are their direct descendants, not many generations removed. We are essentially the same.

The term *positive-sum game* signifies that this system creates more than the sum of its parts. The only real magic – human energy – creates more than it started with. Take some raw materials that are of themselves are of little worth; and when you add human creativity you can create vehicles, computers, and space ships. The materials themselves have been around since the creation of the earth, if they could have turned into something great of themselves they would have done it long ago. But they cannot – it is only when humans manipulate them according to their own ideas that they gain any value. Thus, five dollars worth of materials becomes a product worth thousands of dollars. 

They who do not play the positive-sum game instinctively fall back into being motivated by envy. Ultimately, they find reasons to feel that “there are only so many pieces of the pie.” This is the seed of destruction.

The next thing they say is “if you have a bigger piece of the pie, then someone else has to have less.” That is a zero-sum game – the idea that nothing is really created, just moved from one hand to another. Not only is it false, but it is also the credo of every envious looter who speaks of ‘fairness’ and ‘equal distribution of wealth,’ but who secretly hopes to get a share of wealth held by others.

The real controversy of our time is this: Is human energy allowed to work in the world, or will it be tied down? The miserable experiment of communism has taught the world’s rulers that the positive-sum game is necessary. So, their plan now is to allow human energy to work, but to siphon off as much wealth as possible without killing it all together. We productive people are carrying the governments of the world upon our backs.

Are they worth half of our efforts – half of our lives?

They take half of our earnings away from us continually by a vast web of taxes, fees and regulations – for what benefit? “To help the poor,” they say, and clamorously infer that if you disagree you are a heartless and dangerous person, and further that all will despise you. But if our money is forcibly taken from us, is not the state robbing us? Any dictionary will tell you that this is so, but it is considered poor form to say so – even to consider it.

And are the poor better off? Certainly some of our money goes to the poor (although most is eaten up in the bureaucracy). This feeds their bellies insufficiently, while at the same time locking them into a life of dependence that wages an unending war upon their souls. Is that a good thing? Are the poor better off for this robbing of producers and living in a state of dependency?

Many of you will gasp, and reel in shock that I would challenge the respectability and honor of your tradition, and you fear to let yourselves consider my case. You have come up against someone who does not share in your conspiracy of compliance. You must either turn away from these subjects, or face the prospect of becoming a radical, and of people saying bad things about you.

Are you angry? If so, it is not because I am wrong. If that were the case, you would simply walk away. You are angry because I am ill-mannered enough to bring up subjects that you wish to avoid. My ideas bother you. When they come up, you divert your mind to pat phrases like “that is the price we pay for our society.” You dodge reason, and shunt your thoughts away in order to keep your mental comfort level. You do not face these ideas head-on because you are afraid of them – you are afraid that you might have to agree with them. And then you would have to face the choice either to be a hero or to be a coward.

I stood one evening in IBM Plaza in Chicago, looking over the river-front skyline as the sun sank in the southwest, and realized that the towering monuments to human effort in front of me were the results of the positive sum game run at only half-speed. Chicago was wild and open from the 1830s through the 1890s. Then, slowly, the curbs and limits were imposed by do-gooder government and collectivist types. These inevitably slowed the workings of a city that had been, as one writer said, ‘geared for giants.’ But the restraints were not enough to stop the positive-sum game – only enough to slow it down.

The Chicago skyline I watched was the result of the positive-sum game being played at half-speed, yet its results were awesome. I thought about what might have been if it were allowed to operate unfettered. And then I thought of the greatest example of the positive-sum gave during my lifetime – Hong Kong. It went from rice fields to the grandest city of the east in one generation – an explosion of unrestrained human energy.

What things we have been deprived of! What glorious accomplishments aborted and still-born! And now our recent explosion of technology has become the target of bureaucrats world-wide. Where will we go from here? Will the positive-sum game once again be strangled, or will it migrate to new and open lands?

But! Moving to a new land will be a problem, won’t it? There is no land on this planet that is not claimed by some gang of rulers. So, until cheap space flight is achieved, there is only one new country to be found – cyberspace. So escape there we shall. And there we will – and must, for our own sake and for the sake of our descendants – establish the positive-sum game without restriction.

Toward that end, we have built a private free market. We used our own money to do it, and we’ve broken no laws that we are aware of, save laws that outlaw privacy. Now, the rulers are trying to stop us. Why? We want to run an experiment, and see if freedom really is better than servitude. Why won’t they let us try? Are they interested in the betterment of mankind, or are they really interested in monopoly powers? All we want is to be left alone and to try freedom. Why is that threatening? And why do they wish to imprison us?

*James Farber*

items.title: The Origins of the Y Combinator
items.text:
Ha, you thought this was going to be about *Y Combinator*, the famous startup accelerator, didn't you?  Well, I tricked you, this post is actually gonna be about math.  (But don't worry, at the end it is loosely related to the business).

The "Y Combinator" is a term originating from *lambda calculus*, which, roughly speaking is the "language" mathematicians use to talk about functions.   The term originates from Haskell Curry, though similar ideas were already in circulation by the time he popularized it.

The Y Combinator is a **function that finds the fixed point of any other function**.  That is, the Y combinator is defined with the following relation:

$$YF = F(YF)$$

In words, "Y applied to F" is the same as "F applied to (Y applied to F)".

Why is this useful?  Without getting in to too much detail, it is what allows the lambda notation to describe functions that refer to themselves.  In other words, it allows for *recursive functions*, which can be quite useful in computation.

It can also be used to generate a lot of [paradoxes](https://stacker.news/items/1585258), because it is what lets a function reference itself, and many paradoxes arise from self referentiality.  In fact, Curry called his Y Combinator the "paradoxical combinator".

This self-referential property is what inspired Paul Graham, founder of Y Combinator the startup accelerator, to choose its name.  From the Y Combinator [FAQ](https://www.ycombinator.com/faq):

> Q: Why did you choose the name Y Combinator?
>
> A: The Y combinator is one of the coolest ideas in computer science. It's also a metaphor for what we do. It's a program that runs programs; we're a company that helps start companies.

To be mildly pedantic, the Y Combinator isn't just a program that runs other programs.  It's actually a program that allows *another* program to *run itself*.  In a way, that's even a better description, because an accelerator is a company that helps other companies become self sustaining.

Pretty cool history huh?  Hope this helps you sound smart at parties.

***

Economist bonus:  Fixed points are vitally important in economics.  Not just economics, but any dynamical system.  In fact, every equilibrium is actually a fixed point.

Imagine that $$F$$ describes a rule to transform the state of the world from the current state to the next state, i.e.:

$$X_{t+1} = F X_t$$

The world is in equilibrium if $$X$$ is a fixed point of $$F$$.  That is, if:

$$ X = F X $$

This means that $$X$$ is a world state that stays fixed even after the transformation is applied.

And guess what?  $$ Y F $$ is the fixed point of $$F$$.  So the Y-Combinator by definition lets us find the stable point of any dynamical system.  Or a market equilibrium in economics.

Cool stuff.

items.title: 🌳 Permaculture - American Chestnut a Keystone and my Discovery
items.text:
# Wild Chestnut: a gift of natural capital at the homestead

The American chestnut was a keystone species of the woods but it is effectively extinct after the Chinese chestnut blight ravaged the population over a hundred years ago. Cryphonectria parasitica (chestnut blight). The American chestnut has a fast growing timber form, abundant and consistent nut production, and the combination of the easily decomposing leaves and nurturing canopy creates habitat, sustenance, and fertility for not just wildlife but also for the people of eastern North America.

![](https://i.nostr.build/Wl9KHQK0dCA5jMcNaKa7is.jpg)
*(An extreme example of how large American chestnut trees were in the late 1800s)*

**A Rare Discovery at the homestead**
Here at the homestead, about 7 years ago, I discovered a lucky survivor of the blight. This chestnut tree is mature, producing nuts, and continues to grow!

![](https://i.nostr.build/K3C2BDIPp0Y0h0kSINa7rI.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/TzYgz82XBw63Mh6Gx0aibi.jpg)
The chestnut tree discovery occoured shortly after having some logging done to promote the growth of the sugar maple trees here at the homestead. The pathways the loggers left behind allowed me to easily put up fencing in the woods, which meant I could now keep my horses and rams off the pasture, leaving all the grass growing at the homestead available for feeding ewes and lambs for meat. One day, while doing some work in the woods in the new horse paddock, I found the distinctive chestnut hull and upon further search, some nuts!

![](https://i.nostr.build/9lwn4zPsdGZsY6e3.jpg)
Upon first finding the hills, I thought to myself, where the heck did these come from? A chestnut tree! Where the heck is the chestnut tree? I was looking around horizontally, and saw nothing. Then I looked up to find the chestnut tree towering over me. I spent several more days looking for additional nuts but I must have just gotten lucky with the first few I found. The squirrels beat me to the rest of them. After finding the tree, I quickly came to the realization that if this tree is producing nuts then maybe there are younger trees to found nearby, the offspring.

![](https://i.nostr.build/1z7yRD0CCiEaqszXEwjFxx.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/Royn.jpg)
Sure enough there were! I found a couple young seedlings within 50ft of the tree. One died because it was within the ram paddock and I couldn't protect it from the rams. Eventually they ate it. The second tree, I have been taking care of for several years. It has been nibbled at by the horses and sheep several times but continues to grow. I have yet to eat one chestnut from the large mature chestnut tree, so far I have been trying to sprout them and grow more trees. 

![](https://i.nostr.build/6DFAF1spoHABfbpmzKCVMw.jpg)
Just one year before discovering the wild Chestnut, I choose to plant some hybrid chestnuts I started from seed in the exact area where the mature tree is. I chose that location based on what I read were the ideal growing conditions for chestnut. Sandy light soil. Finding the wild Chestnut tree was confirmation that I had chose the location for the chestnut plantation well!

![](https://i.nostr.build/GX6MVFV6AXmXlyl1Vxmeac.jpg)

While this tree is unlikely a true American chestnut, it's probably some kind of American/European hybrid, the tree has many of the characteristics that made the American chestnut the keystone species that it was. Finding a wild Chestnut tree like this is incredibly rare and a sign to me that I've chose the right place to put down roots and prove to myself that permaculture will lead to a abundant and resilient lifestyle.

items.title: All Ownership is Provisional: Can You Own a Forest? What About a Bitcoin?
items.text:
[*The Natural Dividend*](https://link.amazon/B01NaCYkn) is getting ridiculous now.

I started this project on the recommendation of an [in-depth long read](https://blog.landeconomics.org/p/book-review-the-natural-dividend) about how to think *properly* about nature (https://stacker.news/items/1521292): commodity, property, usage. Basically, a philosophical assessment and discussion around the main economic topics that matter -- scarcity, efficiency, who gets what and why etc etc, how do we coexist and *peacefully cooperate* when we want to use specific things for competing ends.

At first, I found the academic, lefty nature-worshipping lunacy bearable: not nice, not ideal, but the intellectual price I had to pay for admission. 

## 38 pages in, I'm about to tear the pages off their bindings

These (left-wing!) academics are retarded. 

It's getting pretty disgusting. In fact, [given the pair of books](https://stacker.news/items/1587500) by Ben de Waal, a "libertarian" socialist Bitcoiner (yeah, try that one... if you thought *progressive* Bitcoiner was one hell of a contradiction, welcome to this madness), that I embarked on, it's highly relevant. Also, speaking of the monstrosity that is *progressivism* in general:

...**I genuinely think that leftwing-climate-conscious academics have lower cognitive capacities** than the rest of us. Their heads are just not screwed on right -- pun, very much intended. It takes a special amount of PhD lunacy to believe certain things.

On a more serious note: as leftist ideas have **dominated** politics and academia and media for the better part of a century, those of us with a freer persuasion have engaged with and understood the leftist case much better and much deeper than the academic insiders ever have/ever could appreciate e.g., a conservative or libertarian worldview. The asymmetry is painful… even [Jonathan Haidt’s moral foundations framework](https://www.facebook.com/jonathanhaidt/photos/my-colleagues-and-i-revised-moral-foundations-theory-to-do-a-better-job-of-expla/2079950535564617/) [results](https://yukaichou.com/behavioral-analysis/moral-foundations-theory-haidt-care-fairness-loyalty/) are pretty clear on this: conservatives can “speak” more moral languages than progressives can, progressives who are, quite *literally*, less empathetic in the strict meaning of the word. 

Fuck the boomers. Fuck the left. And fuck the academics.

***

## OK, back to business: Can You Own a Forest?

Jonathon Moses and Anne Margrethe Brigham started this [(same!) chapter](https://stacker.news/items/1565551) with a cool, provocative, absurd question about owning the sun. Of course **nobody does (or can) own the sun**, or block anybody else from accessing sunlight (When I mentioned this to Ben in Helsinki, he snarled something like "just wait for it!" or "with enough tech, they will!" again betraying a complete understanding of capital conditions and economic scarcity... **it's not tech or law**, it's E-C-O-N-O-M-I-C-S.)

...

![](https://m.stacker.news/160211)

Of course you can *own a forest*, in precisely the same way you can own a chainsaw.

I have greater **possession** over the chainsaw, seeing as how it's in my basement (which I may or may not, according to these authors' twisted logic, own), and it's smaller in size, so I can physically move it, *possess it* in a way I can't a forest (=doesn't fit in my hand, doesn't have a handle). The forest, however, is out *there* and -- if the stackers will allow the pun -- *rooted in place*. But what do any of those things have to do with ownership?

Ownership (=property) is a social relationship about who gets to do what. More to the point, it's the amount of violence someone exerts on you if you break that ownership bond... steal my chainsaw, let's say; burn down my forest. 

The authors cite Honoré (1961) from an Oxford jurisprudence essay on the 11(!) *incidents* of property but it all comes down to the one single, social-cooperation and social-harmony (shout-out HHH) aspect: **who decides what a good, asset, or thing does when there are rival, mutually exclusive claims/wishes on it?** 
Your car isn't used for the majority of the day/week... what's the reason, economically or philosophically, that [someone else can't "borrow](https://mises.org/free-market/case-hoarding)" it in the meantime? Some worthy cause like a homeless guy napping in there to avoid the rain, let's say. 

Economically speaking, ownership is optionality. Basically: rivalrousness and excludability rule everything. (Which, if you've ever delved down the economic rabbit hole of the social calculation debate as I have, is *the* [components on which everything turn](https://www.mercatus.org/hayekprogram/research/books/rivalry-and-central-planning).)

## Ownership is, like the authors partially outline in this section, the right or first-lien decision on how the item/good/resource is and can be used.

> What we think of as 'private property' in nature is really an abstract bundle of rights that governments grant to individuals or communities. (pp. 36-37)

Ah yes, just how the government owns your house and a government can rescind/take/expropriate any of your stuff at any point.

The fact that they are restricted from doing this by a legal system concerned with whose property is used by whom is SORT OF the definition of a legal order: *rule of law, individual liberty* etc etc. If none of those words have meaning, and the *default* mode of ownership is 100% ruled by the government (who, I'm convinced the authors say while suppressing a laughter, *represent you, the people*), there is no legal order: only (military) might makes right. If so: ***what in the world are we doing here?!***

Look, the fact that a government can rescind or override property claims — practically, physically, militarily, or even "legally" — doesn't invalidate that ownership or property exists (dare I say *precede?!*) irrespective of a government. It doesn't therefore follow that *no* property claims are real; that all ownership is provisional or resort/revert to a government if and when it so chooses.

Or, if you wanna go to that insanity: **Bitcoin.**

By this insane theory (that government owns everything, and it just *lets* you pretend that what is yours is temporarily yours), *nothing* is owned by anybody ever. Oh, but that UTXO somehow refuses to move; you can "own" it all you want, hashtag [New York Finder's Keepers example](https://stacker.news/items/1498602), but it changes nothing about the world. If I hold the private key to a UTXO that you "own" I can move it nonetheless; tell you to royally fuck off in the OP\_RETURN.

As always, Bitcoin stands unique here. Being a commodity without physical dimensions — [element zero, in Knut Svanholm’s phrasing](https://mises.org/mises-wire/sebag-and-natural-money) — it is the first and only thing you can truly own. Not own in a *legal* sense, because Bitcoin, the blockchain, doesn’t care what your laws say: You may have *legal title* to some UTXO, but it matters not.

In fact, and Stephen Kinsella said this directly and uncompromisingly [on stage in Helsinki, too](https://stacker.news/items/1585380): Bitcoin, being *pure information*, cannot be owned. It’s technically and praxeologically speaking just secret information, available and open to all, just accessible to almost nobody.

All you have when you have a UTXO is a highly probabilistic *asymmetric* ability to move funds. Baseline, everyone has some (exceedingly low) probability to spend a given UTXO. You, holding the private key or the seed phrase backup, have a much larger probability — prob-***ability*** — to spend. The entire legalistic edifice of rights goes out the window: it’s *all* ability; possession becoming [ten-tenths of the law.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Possession_is_nine-tenths_of_the_law)

For analogy, my chess brain went to Magnus Carlsen. He has no “right” to win every chess game against chess low-lifes like me; if we were pitted against each other for a trophy, the victory isn’t his *by right*. It’s his by ability: through his superior (asymmetric) information and skill, he will win every time. Just like *your* UTXO is secured by *your* superior ability to move it relative to mine.

***

And when the moronic morons couldn't get worse... *they found a lower low*:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160212)

## Why would (3) be the "default setting," you absolute twatheads?

Or in meme form: **when did** [**this become the default**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ch5_j2q8ZPI)**?!**

If all you wanted to do and say with this book was, *All Your Stuff Are Belong To Us*, then why the hell dress it up like this? How in the world could anybody, for more than a fleeting moment, consider that the *default* ownership position of everything is *the government*?! Plain-old theft and power grabs, masquerading as political philosophy and under the cover of academic intellectualizing.

Fuck.
Right.
Off.

***

Serious retort: I might as well say that (4) — or (1) — is the default setting, and that every government action to restrict, regulate, tax, or otherwise impose on this immaculate conception is in violation of rights and reason.

And stop with this passive-tense hidden-actor nonsense ("...is assigned"): no sex is "assigned" at birth; no income is "distributed" (h/t Rothbard) separately from production; and property rights to goods that are yours are not "assigned" by some prior tribunal, deciding the starting blocks for everyone else.

> As nature belongs to us in common, our representatives in government authorize this private 'taking'. They do this to keep the peace and protect the resources (from either inefficient or over-exploitation), for the benefit of the community they represent. (p. 37)

oh lord. *Please grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change (=other people's moronic ideas and their pathetically limited intellectual stature), and the strength to resist committing the vile damage I wish to inflict upon these fuckheads, ... and perhaps the wisdom to know to which books to direct my attention.*

*TL;DR*: **left-wing people are not impressive; academics are full of it/themselves; this book is the trashiest nonsense bullshit intellectual nonsense I've ever had the misfortune to stumble across (...with the possible exception of the *Capitalism* book.** https://stacker.news/items/1561710**,** https://stacker.news/items/1562148**)**

items.title: Using Bitcoin Miners to Make Maple Syrup
items.text:
Immersion mining with canola oil to concentrate maple sap more quickly
![](https://v.nostr.build/n997.mp4)
I'm using a single S9 hash board immersed in canola oil to heat maple sap to increase the effectiveness of the reverse osmosis sap concentration system.
![](https://i.nostr.build/okkw.jpg)
The weather conditions this season have caused the maple sap to be cold and stay cold which drastically slows down the ability of the RO system to filter water out of it. I ran into a bottle neck where there is more sap than I can keep up with concentrating so I needed to come up with something quickly!
![](https://i.nostr.build/B33D.jpg)
Ideally if the temperature of the sap is 77°f the filter will operate most effectively without damaging the RO membrane. Of course, my mind immediately turned to Bitcoin mining for the heating solution. What I came up with was an immersion system using the homebrew equipment I already had to heat the sap just before it entered the RO. This would allow the majority of the sap to stay cool keeping it from spoiling and still remove the most water possible.
![](https://i.nostr.build/e0Jz.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/aokZ.jpg)
The only thing I didn't have for the immersion system was the dielectric fluid. I had no idea where to find the proper fluid nor did it make sense to pay the high cost for it. The application for this system is very specific and I will only need it until April. I had been joking about using canola oil as dielectric fluid for almost a year but for this situation it seemed like the perfect fit. Canola oil is 70% cheaper than bitcool before shipping and was immediately available!
![](https://i.nostr.build/rDv2.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/J3qq.jpg)
Amazingly, I put everything together and it worked very well without major adjustments. I tip-toed the voltage and frequency of the single S9 hashboard up slowly to find the right balance in temperatures between the two fluid loops. Ultimately, I ended up with an overclocked board drawing over 600w! By the time I got the system setup and dialed in I was already half way through concentrating this collection of sap. The next collection will offer more concrete data on what this system is capable of. For now, even with the worst S9 board I have, I'm getting a 15% rebate on the total power usage of the whole process and it's definitely concentrating sap more quickly. All for ~$10 of canola oil... 👀

items.title: Trip Report: Paris
items.text:
Paris is known for its food and savoir vivre, the art of living your life. It comes as no surprise that the merchants I found accepting Bitcoin in Paris are all serving foods and drinks, and so this trip report is almost more of a food review than a Bitcoin review.

🧆In the hip 18th arrondissement lies Chez Ginette, a fairly typical cafe with its seats facing the trottoir, so Parisians can watch each other. The menu offers all the classic dishes you would expect from a place like this, but somehow lacks a theme or specialization. I order the greatest classic there is, the steak tartare. It comes préparé, meaning the raw egg is mixed in. It's definitely of high quality and I'm also happy about the pommes frites on the side. There is a "Bitcoin Lightning payments accepted" sticker on the door, and as I ask to pay with Bitcoin the waiter does not hesitate, although it takes him a while to get his colleague to come over with an orange point of sale terminal running the Swiss Bitcoin Pay app, built on BTCPay. The payment goes through almost instantly.

🍸Le Greffulhe is another cafe close to the opera and a high-end fashion district. As I arrive I mistake a man standing by the entrance for staff and ask him about Bitcoin paymnets. He says he would be surprised if they did, and indeed he is after we go inside together to ask the cashier. The cafe belongs to the same category as Chez Ginette, but the atmosphere feels very different, and although they do serve food, I never got the chance to try it during my two visits. Instead I had Aperol Spritz and Campari Soda, and payments went smoothly to the mobile phone of the cashier, also running Swiss Bitcoin Pay.

🍺Undoubtedly the heart of the Paris Bitcoin community is N'importe Quoi near Les Halles, somewhat in the geographical center of the city. The dive bar has the kind of anarchic and old-school feminist feel of a place that you almost expect to be taking Bitcoin. I'm here quite early and all by myself, and at first the bar tender denies my Bitcoin payment, saying "usually we do." Eventually she shows mercy with me and digs up the phone that has fallen somewhere behind the cash register, presumably only kept for the sole purpose of processing Bitcoin payments. The bar also uses Swiss Bitcoin Pay, and I'm quite pleased with how fast I can find a route to their node, and how I never paid more than 0.09% in fees, just a few sats.

🍝The Italian restaurant Costa d'Amalfi greets visitors with a warning: No Pizza. Connoisseurs will recognize this as a sign of quality, and indeed the family-run trattoria is exactly the kind of place you typically see accepting Bitcoin in Italy. Everything is well curated, the menu is short and specializes in one thing: truffle dishes. The owner comes over to talk to me about Bitcoin, telling me stories of his family and his Bitcoin story. He also uses the now familiar Swiss Bitcoin Pay and is quite happy with it.

🥮Located near Volontaires, an hommage to the volunteer soldiers of the French Revolution, is one of the areas of Paris known for their contemporary bohème lifestyle. Le Drapeau de la Fidélité fits it perfectly with its nondescript facade and carefully curated interior. There are plenty of books that make the restaurant feel more like a library, and they appear to have actually been read frequently. There are antiques, paintings, signed letters and a banner proclaiming a "Universal Humanist Capitalist Society" that I cannot find any other information about. The owner, a well-dressed older Vietnamese gentleman appears to run the tiny restaurant with its maybe 12 seats together with his son. The menu is short and the dishes simple and affordable. I order the porc caramélisé and pay a round 18,000 satoshi. The owner seems quite pleased with me paying with Bitcoin, which is always a great feeling when spending it. He uses Cake wallet, but doesn't know how to set an amount for his invoices. Also, his wallet is priced in USD, meaning I have to look up the rate on my end. As far as routing fees go, it's by far my most expensive payment at 0.3%.

🍷Near the Gare d'Austerlitz I visit La Brasserie L'Audièrnes. The area seems to be very popular with students, and everyone at the bar seems to be talking about AI, with many conversations in English. I order my drink at the bar and pay right away, but the cashier is hesitant to show me his wallet, and instead asks his colleague over. We navigate through the interface of some unfamiliar crypto wallet, and all we can find is an onchain address, which I pay to reluctantly.

I'm quite happy with my visit to Paris and especially the Bitcoin places that I found. I love the opportunity to find some random or hidden gems in the city that I would have never been able to visit if it weren't for Bitcoin. I love talking to the staff and the owners, there is always something to learn, and sometimes to teach, about how people are using Bitcoin. I also went to six other places, four of which were closed, and two of which no longer accept Bitcoin. At one of these places, the doors and cash register covered in Bitcoin stickers, I was practically laughed at for asking to pay with Bitcoin, before being asked to pay one Bitcoin to buy everyone a round. Finally one reason to implement BIP 177.

items.title: [Read-along] The Odyssey, W.H.D. Rouse, Books I - III
items.text:
*Below I am starting the book club, as promised previously. It has probably taken longer than I originally led on. I expect that this can be forgiven. Whether you took up the challenge or not, there may be something for you in the following post. I have made an effort to give some original thoughts, followed by a character list and book summaries. As mentioned before, I am reading a hard copy of the translation of W.H.D. Rouse, but I can also recommend the* [*digitized version of the translation of A.S. Kline.*](https://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odhome.php)

***

# leading themes and ideas

* post-war society leads to excess and decay
* culture, values, family, country -- all need to be defended by their inheritors
* the most commonly held belief is not always the correct one

# Commentary

The first three books show how Telemachos has been living and responding to the apparent death of his father, Odysseus. Unbeknownst to Telemachos, his father is lost at sea, dealing with cyclops, and upsetting Poseidon in the meantime. With the help of other greek heroes (Achilles, Agememnon, Nestor, Menelaus etc.), Odysseus led the Achaeans to victory at the battle of Troy, and since then, things have not been going so well back home. This is the setup for the poem.

This is a story of what happens in the aftermath of war, when a great society produces heroes that defend its culture and norms against outsiders, and how, despite their victory on the battlefield, this same culture must be defended in their absence. This is seen at the outset, when the gods discuss what has become of the house of Atreus, whose son, Agememnon, finds himself the victim of Agisthos. The latter is eventually murdered by Agememnon's own son, Orestes, in an act of revenge for the murder of his father and the destruction of his household. Zeus laments the fact that, although they have brought this terrible fate upon themselves, men continue to hold Zeus to account. Wherever the fault lay, the poem tries to reckon with the phenomenon where society grows weak in the absence of the warriors who will defend their culture.

As the drama of the poem ensues, it is revealed how political infighting led the Achaeans to split up after Troy, leaving Agememnon and Odysseus away from their homeland. In the latter's absence, his wife Penelope and his son Telemachos have been left to defend what is left of his household. Suitors consume Odysseus' wealth, as they loiter, courting Penelope.

**So far, I have taken the following from the poem, summarized in a few sentences:**

* A great culture, such as the Greeks had, will produce great warriors, in whose absence its greatness will quickly fall to shambles.
* There will always be those willing to feast on the spoils bought by the sweat and blood of another person's brow
* Even when an entire population believe one thing, it may not be true. Truth is not easily discerned, but found out through persistence, struggle and adventure.

So, to you, reader of Epic poetry, I ask the question:

* Where do you see yourself on this cycle (i.e. good times --> weak men --> bad times --> strong men?)
* Is there an analogue in modern culture to the suitors feasting on Odysseus' wealth?

***

# Reading notes:

key characters

* Odysseys: a great warrior from Ithica. Never returned from the battle of Troy, in which he earned his stripes as a hero.
* Telemachos: the son of Odysseus.
* Penelope: the wife of Odysseus. Awaiting Odysseus' return.
* Suitors: men gathered in Ithica, enjoyers of Odysseus' house and belongings, as they vie for Penelope's hand in marriage.
* Zeus: Father of the gods. Feels let down by mortal men because of what happened in the aftermath of the battle of Troy concerning Agememnon.
* Aigisthos: killed Agememnon and married his wife. Is then killed by the latter's son, Orestes.
* Agememnon: in the aftermath of the battle of Troy, did not wish to sail home, for fear of displeasing Athena. He splits from Diomedes and Nestor, and stays in Troy
* Athena: Zeus' daughter. Favors Odysseus, intervenes for him so as not to see his house come into ruin
* Poseidon: god of the seas
* Mentes/Mentor: Athena in the form of a man, advises Telemachos in Ithica and in Pylos.
* Aigyptios: Wise councilman, blesses Telemachos
* Nestor: son of Neleus, king of Pylos.

# Book Summaries:

## Book I

> These men amuse themselves with music and song, freely, since they consume another’s wealth without repayment, one whose white bones are tumbling in the waves, or rotting in the rain on some far shore
> \--Mentes.

Zeus and Athena meet on Olympus. Lament Agememnon's murder and betrayal by Aigisthos. Athena descends from Olympus to intervene into the affairs of Telemachos, to keep him from a similar fate. His father, Odysseus, suffers the ire of Poseidon, who keeps him from returning home against the will of the other gods. Suitors, who think Odysseus is dead, harass Penelope and Telemachos, and take advantage of the latter's good manners. No one really knows whether Odysseus has died. Telemachos answers Mentes that he does not stop the suitors from courting his mother for the dread of not knowing what has come of his father. Before transforming into a bird to depart, Athena rouses Telemachos to gather the lords together and order them to stop, and moreover, that he should go out in search of his father.

## Book II

> ‘My lords, my Suitors, though Odysseus is dead and you are eager for me to marry, have patience till I complete this work, I do not want it wasted, this shroud for noble Laertes, ready for when pitiless death’s cruel end overtakes him: since I fear some Achaean woman of this land would blame me, if he who won great wealth lay there without a shroud.’
> \--Penelope

Telemachos assembles the lords of Ithica and makes his case, demanding that and end be put to the suitors' behavior. Antinous rebukes him, saying that Penelope has tricked them for the past three years, by saying she would choose a husband when the finishes weaving the shroud of Odysseus' father, Laertes, which she would work on during the day only to unravel the work she had completed under the darkness of night. Zeus sends an omen portending the destruction of the suitors. Athena again urges Telemachos to go in search of his father, provisions a ship and a crew for him, and even afflicts the suitors in Telemachos' home with drowsiness. Telemachos sets sail for Pylos in search of news of his father.

## Book III

Telemachos arrives at Pylos, where the people all pay sacrifice to the gods. Telemachos and Mentor make an offering to Poseidon, in Nestor's name. Telemachos appeals to Nestor, who also fought at Troy, to give news of what happened to Odysseus. He reports that the latter was caught in the middle of a feud between Menelaus, who wished to depart after the battle of Troy, and Agememnon, who feared the angering the gods, and wished to wait. Nestor and Odysseus went with Menelaus, leaving Agememnon behind. In a moment of hesitation, however, Odysseus turned back to join Agememnon. Nestor and Menelaus sail from Troy together and in the meantime, Aigisthos overtakes Agememnon, killing him and taking his wife for marriage. Nestor urges Telemachos to look on the heroism of Orestes, who took revenge against and murdered his father's murderer, Aigisthos. He tells Telemachos he needs to visit Menelaus for news of what came of Odysseus. Nestor offers Telemachos his men and ships, his hospitality, they sacrifice a heifer to Athena, and set off at dawn.

![](https://i.nostr.build/Bl2VhTfRzigPZBS3.jpg)
The 40ish birds are working 4 compost piles every day, breaking them down and consuming as many worms and fly larvae as the can find.
![](https://i.nostr.build/iNdM1gBA4b9vO85C.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/1FYWKfVTojZYynTg.jpg)
Each day I spend 20 minutes rebuilding the piles and watering them with nutrient rich water from the duck bath. Then I spend 20 minutes collecting as much fresh horse manure as I can, adding it to the system. With each rebuilding of the piles, they march slowly forward from the back of the paddock to the front. By the time the pile reaches the front the compost is finished and ready for use around the homestead. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/MbGXG22ZdoocGVU6.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/jh60ABOg7vAYpU2V.jpg)
While I do some work to maintain the energy flow through the system, the chickens are doing good work on the piles, consuming horse fly larvae reducing the pest pressure on the horses, and paying me in eggs for the work. Meanwhile I'm feeding them less and less grain. We are producing yeilds beyond what we can utilize at the homestead so I've been selling the compost and eggs at Bitcoin meetups in my area. Distributing natural capital and strengthening my local Bitcoin culture and community. A great example of a permaculture system here at the homestead!

items.title: Why SoV -> MoE -> UoA for bitcoin
items.text:
I shared [an article](https://stacker.news/items/1582356/r/Undisciplined) about how things in the past have emerged as money. In brief the story is that commonly valued things (like salt, for instance) were easy to use for indirect exchange because almost everyone used them and that led to thinking in terms of how much you could exchange your salt for or how much salt you could attain for your goods (unit of account) and finally converting less storable goods into salt for future exchange (store of value).

The order seems to be different for bitcoin and people generally seem to accept that the order will be store of value (SoV), followed by medium of exchange (MoE), followed by unit of account (UoA). Why is that? I don't think anyone's written out the reasoning for ~bitcoin_beginners, although many of us probably have the same, or similar, understanding.

The short answer is that bitcoin obviously *can be* used for exchange, even if it isn't a prevailing MoE, and the hard supply cap makes it seem like a better money for savings than inflationary fiat currencies. In other words, people are taking it seriously as a money (even if only implicitly) and considering where it has the strongest advantage over other currencies.

That means the path to hyperbitcoinization will most likely look like

1. Commonly used as a store of value because fiat sucks hardest at that. As this progresses, the monetary premia of other assets (homes, fine art, precious metals, etc.) will be increasingly absorbed by bitcoin, resulting in much greater purchasing power.
2. Once bitcoin is the preferred savings technology, people will prefer receiving it in exchanges. That preference combined with bitcoin's lower transactions costs should lead to discounts for costumers willing to pay in bitcoin. That will further increase the purchasing power of bitcoin.
3. Only once bitcoin is commonly used for exchange will people do their accounting in bitcoin and denominate contracts in terms of bitcoin. Prior to that point, I suspect people will need to do mixed accounting where they keep track of their fiat and bitcoin income and expenses separately.

Is that roughly how everyone else sees events unfolding?

items.title: Why Were Victorian Elites so Effective? (Works in Progress Magazine, Sam Hughes)
items.text:
## Amazing (long) read, highly recommend

I like Works in Progress. *A lot*. It's a serious outlet for long-form journalism, and it (usually!) features writers whose minds are oriented correctly toward the future. (its editor-in-chief lost his mind during 'rona, so I've stayed away from reading/subscribing or even attempting to contribute... *but I'm often very tempted*)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160670)

## What's the Key For Success?

Work hard, long hours, education, 5am, cold plunges, diversity, pay your politicians well to avoid corruption *blah-blah*?

No, no:

> The elites of Victorian Britain operated differently. Their schools and universities were not terribly academic and had very little STEM. As adults, **they got up late, drank a lot, and spent a remarkable share of their waking hours partying.** They loved feasting, sports, holidays, dancing, and dressing up. Contrary to their stodgy reputation, they were probably a lot of fun.

> the elites of nineteenth-century Britain were, by their own lights, extremely successful. For much of the century, Britain was the richest country on Earth. Its companies dominated global commerce, industry and finance.

## In Defence of Debauchery

![](https://m.stacker.news/160674)

* **SCHOOLING:** while strict (early age, regulated times, single-sex away from family, corporal punishment), the values the English Victorian elite cultivated at boarding school were remarkably progressive: loyalty, internationalism, studies of the arts -- Latin and Ancient Greek --

Amazing:

> There was **resistance to the teaching of science, not because Victorians were hostile to science** in principle, but because they thought it **irrelevant to the kind of moral and cultural formation** that a school for gentlemen was supposed to provide.
> (By contrast, girls were not usually taught classics, meaning that, rather surprisingly, affluent Victorian girls generally followed a more modern curriculum than their brothers.)

While not obviously successful, it cultivated valuable skills:

> ...The most that can be said for Victorians’ classical education is perhaps that, like schooling in any difficult subject, it trained students in self-discipline, memorization, and applying rules.

And *this* we could definitely learn from today:

> Under such circumstances, it is perhaps unsurprising that the share of time spent in the classroom was relatively modest. At Rugby School, weeks were divided into three ‘full days’, three ‘half days’, and Sunday. On a full day, students spent about five hours in the classroom, compared with maybe two hours on a half day.  \[AND, importantly:] They also tended to be shorter than those of contemporary elite schools in France, Germany, or Italy, where the curriculum was normally more academically rigorous.

## "Victorians thought extremely highly of sports, believing that they instilled team spirit and endurance, fostered mutual loyalty, channeled energy and competitiveness, and taught men how to win and lose graciously."

One Loretto School headmaster described the school's priorities: **1) character, 2) physique,** 3) intelligence, 4) manners, 5) information. First time *brawns > brains, eh*

* **UNIVERSITIES**: Not much studying, plenty of "teambuilding"

I found *this* observation interesting:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160677)

> Oxbridge tutors believed overwhelmingly that the purpose of an undergraduate degree was not training for work nor even preparation for academic research, but rather a general moral and intellectual formation that would fit students for any professional role they might later pursue.

also:

> Fellowships were opened up to laymen in the later decades of the century, but **Oxford and Cambridge did not become world-leading research institutions until they were transformed by German scholars fleeing Nazism in the 1930s.** The dominance of Oxbridge in British culture was unusual: these institutions educated a much larger share of the elite than was the case for any two institutions in any other country

Fuck, these peeps just had *great* lives. (In some respects, Oxford life these days is very similar!)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160679)

* **ADULTHOOD**: Busy-busy-fucking busy bee... but not in the way you think

## "One virtue that upper-class Victorian education signally failed to inculcate was early rising. Although Victorian schoolboys and university students got up fairly early for chapel, the day of an upper-class Victorian adult started late."

Fuck *yeah!* Den loves victory https://stacker.news/items/1590741

The great statesmen and prime ministers back then "breakfasted at 9 am" or hosted a "social breakfast starting at 10.30 am (claret was served), continuing till about noon." **A-M-A-Z-I-N-G**

Also, not that different from today (minus the frock)

> general, however, Britain’s elites were slow to suburbanize, and in 1914 most still lived in centrally located row houses and walked to work. Every day a great herd of frock-coated men emerged from Belgravia and Mayfair and poured through Covent Garden to their offices in Parliament, Whitehall, the Inns of Court, and the City.

If you've noticed the drinking *at every goddamn meal*, you're not alone. It's pretty disturbing, an entire nation run by high-functioning alcoholics.

> The Victorians loved drinking and drank a lot by modern standards. Men drank more than women, but women drank a good deal too: one conduct guide[noted that](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/12426/pg12426-images.html)‘young ladies seldom drink more than three glasses of wine at dinner but married ladies, professional ladies, and those accustomed to society, and habits of affluence, will habitually take five or even six, whether in their own homes or at the tables of their friends’.

...and the partying, until the wee hours. Plus, for some odd reason Americans call this "Irish exit" (or French goodbye):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160682)

And they were hardly just for entertainment:

> the social events of the Victorian elite were notable for their lack of segregation by age or sex. A Society ball discharged the functions of both a teenage house party and a business networking convention: in fact, it*was* both a teenage house party and a business networking convention. \[...] Unmarried young people (and their unfortunate parents) might go to three or four balls per week, while other Society members would go to one or two. But the other nights were scarcely less busy. Opera, theatre and concerts were important, especially opening or gala nights.

Fuck, dudes kept busy.

> An MP might miss dinner for a late sitting of Parliament, but still drop into a soirée at 10.30pm, turn up to a supper party at 11.45pm, and then arrive at a ball at 1am. From February to July, the Victorian upper class led a remarkably nocturnal existence, with bedtimes in the small hours and the mornings something of a write-off.

## "All else being equal, rich and powerful Victorians must have been less productive for spending four hours a day in the office rather than twelve. But the creation of a single ruling *Gemeinschaft* may have had compensatory advantages."

Domestic and international (geo)political implications:

> This obviously had advantages for Britain. The elites of the American South had a very different identity to those of the North, and ultimately led the country into civil war. Spain, Italy and France suffered from incessant conflicts between urban bourgeois and rural nobility. Germany was riven with strife along geographical, religious, and class lines. **Some of these tensions existed in Britain, but except in Ireland, the elite finessed them peacefully.**

## "Would modern societies work better if their local and national government were conducted by a tight-knit community of extremely rich and successful people?"

The author thinks not... but a kid can dream, longing as we do for the best moment in (modern) Western civilization: the Victorian era.
