items.title: Swing and a miss: Paying with Bitcoin on a Square Terminal
items.text:
This year, I've got my kids doing a homeschool co-op two days a week. This just means that a group of homeschool parents have organized to teach their children in a group setting, and possibly hire a teacher or two for subjects where more formal education might be helpful (languages, music, science?). 

Unfortunately, the coop we have joined is quite some way from our home, so after dropping off the children, I go to a nearby coffee shop to work -- a coffee shop that has a Square terminal.

I have asked if they accept Bitcoin a number of times so far, but in all cases the cashier's answer has been "I don't think so" or "I'll have to talk to the person who manages this" (pointing at the terminal). It's a busy place and so there is often a line, and I haven't wanted to try to make anyone wait while I help figure out how to turn on Bitcoin payments, and so I haven't made much progress. 

Today, the person behind the cash register was the owner and I seized my opportunity. 

I placed my order and while he was ringing it up, I said, "I've heard that these Square terminals accept bitcoin."

The owner glanced up at me and said, "I've heard that, too. Let's see if we can figure it out."

This was a much more enthusiastic response than I was expecting. He poked away at the terminal for a few minutes and then said, "I think it only takes bitcoin if you have CashApp."

I told him that this was not the case, but that if he could get it to display a QR code I could try paying that.

He continued to tap on the terminal without much effect. I should say this terminal was not the sort that has a rotatable screen. There is one fixed screen facing the cashier and a smaller fixed screen facing the customer. This was showing the message "Waiting for cashier..."

"I think you have to tap to pay," he said.

Now, I don't use any of the Lightning wallets that have implemented tap to pay (as far as I remember there aren't very many) so that wasn't an option. I told him that I needed a QR code to scan.

After another couple minutes, the owner volunteered: "Maybe I can text it to you." 

I am usually loathe to provide a phone number, but in the interest of dismantling the legacy financial system, I gave it to him. I immediately received a text with a link. The link was to pay for my coffee, but had required fields for name, phone number, and email. At the bottom I saw a green button that said pay with CashApp or something like that. I tapped it, but nothing happened because I had not entered the required fields. 

Still in the interest of taking down the fiat empire, I entered some incorrect information in these fields. But then when I tapped the green button, it presented me with a message informing me that I did not have CashApp and a button to download CashApp. 

At this point the line behind me was long enough that I offered to pay with cash and the owner accept with some visible signs of relief.

So: I have failed on this the fourth time I've tried to pay with Bitcoin at this Square terminal. I suspect that the owner needs to turn Bitcoin payments on and that I will need to talk him through this process, so I'll have to rewatch those videos about how to do this. 

It occurs to me that Square could do a lot better with this flow if they had a button that allowed the cashier to display a QR code that was simultaneously a CashApp code and a Lightning invoice. This is a lot to ask, but I'm pretty sure it needs to be at least that easy for it to work well.

items.title: How to Get People to Use Bitcoin
items.text:
For many years, I’ve been trying to figure out how to get bitcoin into people’s hands. Even long-time bitcoiners often don’t want to pay with bitcoin. At best, they slowly accumulate it, and they don’t really feel like they’re missing anything. They buy it on exchanges, pay fees, expose their personal information, and need a third party’s blessing for every transaction.

I sometimes hear people say that bitcoin doesn’t need anyone and that, on the contrary, we need bitcoin. I see it a little differently. To me, bitcoin is something like a living organism. I consider its creation to be an event almost as rare as the emergence of life itself. But for bitcoin to truly live and serve us as better money, I believe it needs users.

With every transaction, a new connection is created or an existing one is strengthened. Users gradually get better at securing their bitcoin, demand better tools, and bitcoin becomes more resilient.

That’s why I don’t think adoption is some kind of optional bonus.
**Adoption is a fundamental condition for bitcoin to actually be useful.**

## I tried various approaches

* I liked the idea of bringing bitcoin directly into Signal, for example: https://stacker.news/items/85702
  * But Signal still hasn’t added bitcoin support, and I’m afraid there simply isn’t enough incentive for them to do so anytime soon.
* Years ago, I also created an app that allowed people to load bitcoin onto an NFC card and pass it around much like cash: https://stacker.news/items/117623
  * Technically, it worked. But there wasn’t enough interest. It was a nice project, but it didn’t solve a real problem for people.
* Later, I also looked into why even bitcoiners themselves often don’t want to pay with bitcoin: https://stacker.news/items/210830

## It’s not enough to let merchants accept bitcoin

In the meantime, I onboarded dozens of businesses and bitcoiners locally.

Most of them were just isolated points on a map. A business started accepting bitcoin, but nobody actually paid with it. Eventually, the merchant forgot how to accept a bitcoin payment or what to do with the bitcoin they received.

It wasn’t until about a year ago that I managed to partially break through this problem.

I onboarded another business simply because we went there regularly. And to this day, every week we come there in a changing group of people, with everyone paying in bitcoin. https://stacker.news/items/1584550

![](https://m.stacker.news/159586)

The pub owner didn’t want bitcoin at all in the beginning. What matters to him is us as customers who come to his pub because of bitcoin. In the end, a merchant will accept pretty much any form of payment. What’s more important is finding people who are willing to pay with bitcoin.

Here, we use bitcoin also as a filter for finding interesting people. Anyone willing to pay with bitcoin is kind of open-minded, and it’s a pleasure to get to know them over a regular lunch.

## I don’t want to depend on a single app again

Over the years, I’ve recommended various wallets and tools to people. Some of them eventually disappeared.

The custodial version of Wallet of Satoshi, which was the most popular one, stopped working. Alza, the largest retailer in the Czech Republic and one of the first major merchants to accept bitcoin, started requiring additional administrative steps when paying with bitcoin. Qerko, which allowed bitcoin payments at around 1,000 businesses, removed bitcoin support.

At first, this was pretty discouraging. It was the end of 2025, and at the same time the price of bitcoin dropped significantly. I had to figure out what to do with the dozens of people I had introduced to a particular app, which was now no longer going to work for them.

I felt a little trapped. With every app, there was a risk that I would have to repeat the whole migration process again at any time.

But in January 2026, it also seemed to me that AI models had improved significantly, so I decided to try building my own wallet. One that I had been carrying around in my head for years.

## Linky

Linky is a bitcoin wallet and, at the same time, a communication layer for the people you want to use bitcoin with.

You can add your contacts, send them messages and bitcoin. You can pay any Lightning invoice. You can load bitcoin in the form of Cashu tokens onto an NFC card or send it to someone in a message — even to someone who doesn’t use Linky at all.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159587)

But I’m also trying to build a certain degree of antifragility into it.

From the beginning, I’ve been building Linky so that the app doesn’t depend on a particular operator. There are already other instances running on different domains. If my instance stopped working tomorrow, the network wouldn’t necessarily have to disappear with it.

We achieve this through a combination of three decentralized technologies:

* **Cashu** for bitcoin,
* **Nostr** for communication,
* **Evolu** for data storage.

We use several other interesting technologies as well, but I don’t want to get into the technical details here. There are now six other developers working on Linky. One of them is a close friend of mine who has been improving the app very intensively, primarily on the technical side.

What started as a funny vibecoded app is gradually becoming a serious project.

Around 250 people are currently testing Linky in the local group, and several hundred more users are using it.

## Individuals

People use Linky because they like it.

Thanks to its simplicity and steadily increasing reliability, it is gradually becoming the primary bitcoin wallet for many people.

**However, most people still don’t actually need a lightning wallet.** 😢

You can build a great wallet. You can onboard merchants. You can explain the benefits of bitcoin to people.
But if they have no reason to use bitcoin, all of those things will remain just flashes of activity.

## Proxy Payments

Recently, however, we managed to create a feature that I think can at least partially solve this problem. We call it **proxy payments**.

In the Czech Republic, people increasingly use QR codes for bank transfers. You can find them in online shops as well as physical stores.

For users, this is still somewhat less convenient than paying by card, but merchants love it because they don’t have to pay card-network fees.

Today, I can pay with bitcoin at any of these businesses. No fees and no KYC.

I scan the payment QR code using Linky - just as if I were paying a lightning invoice. Linky offers me the option to send the payment request to my contacts.

I select several friends and send them the offer.

Whoever accepts it first receives the payment details from the QR code. They pay the merchant from their bank account, and I send them sats in return.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159589)

## Does it worth the effort?

Maybe this sounds like a pointless detour. Why would I ask someone else to pay by bank transfer on my behalf when I could simply pay myself?

For me, it’s useful because I don’t have to hold fiat that is losing value.

For my friends, it’s useful because they don’t have to use an exchange, pay fees, or expose their personal information. They acquire bitcoin in an interactive way — usually in small amounts.

As a side benefit for everyone, there is the more abstract fact that you are building the bitcoin network and thereby helping ensure that you’ll be able to use bitcoin in the future as well.

To use proxy payments comfortably, you need roughly two or three people. Most payments are completed within two minutes. It’s not as direct or fast as paying by card, but it works surprisingly well.

Linky is showing people new ways to use bitcoin.

**Come help us test and build our shared bitcoin network. 🙏**

items.title: Bank Runs are Good, Actually: Death to the Central Banks (FT, Toby Nangle)
items.text:
ASTONISHING piece to see in regular financial press. *Maybe the tide is turning and the world is healing?*

![](https://m.stacker.news/159395)

The basic/most fundamental rationale for a central bank isn't financing the gov deficit (which they don't...*ish*) or set centralized interest rates, but to support commercial banks when faced with bank runs (=stand ready to lend against their assets, even if distressed, with newly created base money, so stave off the run.) The idea, from Francis Barings to Diamond\&Dybvig's [Nobel Prize](https://stacker.news/items/1583458?commentId=1583534) winning article, is that depositors are fickle and might/will run on perfectly healthy banks *and* that such runs cause real damage to the economy (*and* might spread through the banking system like wildfire and we all collapse into Great Depression 2.0).
*That's everything that's wrong with monetary economics and politics around central banks in one sentence...*

***

The authors of the paper Nangle discusses here used the Chronicling America project, scanned newspapers, then...

> they used LLMs to sift these articles further to find pieces about actual bank runs rather than, say, stuff about boats running into river banks, or the local bank manager running for mayor, and to match each report to individual banks.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159396)

> According to Verner, the research reveals that the idea that runs kill solvent banks is dramatically overstated. It turns out that depositors are actually pretty good at working out how dodgy a bank is, generally making runs on banks that are insolvent or very close to insolvent.

This is incredible. Specifically, — and I'm sparing you a deep dive into debates in financial history and monetary economics here — a big rationale for *why central banks must exist* is **to prevent bad types of bank runs.**

Running a bank means it has to shed assets, assets that aren't "finished," or turned into workable projects and thus liqudity, yet. (That's sort of the purpuse of a bank: to *liquify* illiquid assets, hold the maturity and duration mismatch in the meantime.)  Selling these assets quickly means taking (large) haircuts on book value, meaning a random run on a healthy bank can destroy projects or at least turn the bank itself bankrupt -- destroying customer relatioships and disrupting the bank-money-level money supply etc etc. 
**That's all unnecessary, and a benevolent central bank/observer can improve upon the state of the world by injecting more money and support the healthy bank.**

## ...except, depositors don't run on healthy banks!

That's what this beautiful history and database shows. Somehow, depositors (in aggregate) are clever enough to sniff out when something is wrong *and not* structurally/mindlessly/sunspot-style make erratic and concentrated mistakes.

If you scratch [the lender or last resort literature a little](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/when-did-the-bank-of-england-become-a-lender-of-last-resort/), you find that it's a good, disciplining market mechanism for depositors to run on banks. Here's a schematic:

* if bank is healthy and other bankers know it, then the bank can source enough liquidity from them ("recycling" deposits), against a very minimal short-term expense. **No problem, no negative outcome, no need for lender of last resort** 
* if the bank is unhealthy and the other bankers know it, they won't lend to it and it will fail, *and it will be a good thing!* Bankers taking bad risks or making bad investments should fail, like every other business in a market economy.
* if the bank is healthy, but the **other bankers don't know it** *and so refuse to lend*, that's when a lender of last resort needs to step in and save the day. By supplying that extra liquidity it can stave off the damaging run and everyone is better off for it.

Here's the best short article/overview I've ever seen on this (by [George Kaufman, for econlib](https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/BankRuns.html)):

![](https://m.stacker.news/159394)

---

The literature on bank runs and central banks is basically an exercise in showing **whether or not the central bank knows about the true state of a given bank better than other bankers do.**

When central banks *also* had prudential obligation, by chance some of its workers would have recently audited and inspected private information for that bank, meaning it's quite plausible that central bankers *do* have some insider information here that they can act on. (Nowadays that function is usually separated to another agency, thus the argument is practically quite moot.)

But... If historically and practically depositors are good enough in aggregate to sniff out what's wrong, there's no *need* for a central bank to intervene and override their market choice.

Bank runs are bad for local economies

> ...only if the banks that are being abandoned have been making bad loans, a big borrower defaults, or something like that.

...in which case there is **a real economic loss that we want/need someone to carry** — not paper over and pretend it's not there. (\_cough\_, Bitfinex...)

***

Told yah:

> Surely **the mere process of a run on a healthy bank wreaked havoc on their local economy?** Apparently not.

> Cross-referencing each bank’s financial strength, the researchers trace the local economic impact of each bank run using Bradstreet’s contemporary reporting. They find that a run on a strong bank doesn’t really impose any economic cost at all on the local economy. Yet runs on banks whose fundamentals are awful are followed by major lending contractions that can cause all sorts of spillover problems.

and:

> Out of **3,984 bank runs on individual US banks from 1863–1934**, the authors identify 53 that look like they’re based on “misinformation” or “depositor confusion”, which reads as academese for “blind panic”. Of these 53 oddities, six banks failed, which sounds like maybe six too many. But the researchers argue that the historical data indicates that “strong banks (fundamentals in the upper tercile) subject to **non-fundamental runs have a zero probability of failure”**
> one of the footnotes indicates that at least one of these failed banks had basically committed massive fraud, which was only uncovered by their so-called irrational run.

*Even that*, the depositors sniffed out. Amazing.

***

All "pretty interesting" says Nangle, understating the explosive result.

> the ideas that the Nobel winners formalise are really the ones sitting behind the rationale for bank deposit insurance.

Yes. This evidence shows/weighs heavy that lender of last resort is a defunct and unnecessary function — liable to abuse, nepotism, and trigger-happy rulers, not actually saving a banking system that needs it

items.title: How life gets in the way of Stacker News
items.text:
I’ve been largely offline and not really on SN much these days. Mostly a collection of small things, like health issues that aren’t in the “oh shit” realm, but which take up lots of time and energy (neither my wife nor I have figured out how to stop getting older - other than the one obvious one - and that means more health bullshit each day, apparently). Plus work just being, well, work. And assorted miscellaneous things. Much as I love SN, I only have so much time in a given day.

But this in turn has made it clear how much I need a better subscription page for SN. When I do have time for SN, I hit my subscription page and it’s fucking overwhelming. If I’m lucky, I can see maybe twelve hours worth of stuff, but sometimes, it’s only a few hours.

I subscribe to maybe eight territories, and maybe as many individual posters. But that’s enough (especially as some of the territories have gotten busier) to completely overwhelm my feed. I’ve missed plenty of important posts ([one costing me 10K sats](https://stacker.news/items/1571441) [^1]), and plenty more where I’d have loved to contributed to discussions.

One obvious solution would be to just reduce what I subscribe to. But that’s self-defeating. I subscribe to people and communities because I like them and want updates. I also (obviously) want notifications on posts I make and when I’m tagged.

What I’d like (and I have no idea if this is on the radar, nor if it’s easy/possible) is the ability to break up my subscription page. The aggregate page is fine when I’m on a lot. But when I’m not, allow me to see territory subscriptions from separately from the user subscriptions separately from the comments on my actual posts. I could manually just change all my settings each time, but if I had the time to do all that all the time, I’d have the time to keep up with my feeds. As it stands, having a lack of time to keep up with SN is, in itself, something that causes me to fall behind even further on SN.

I'm always reluctant to request features/changes that may only help me, but putting this out there as something that others who are short on time (assuming I'm not the only person whose entire life doesn't revolve around SN) might also want to weigh in on?

[^1]: Not really, since I’d have lost eventually, and probably soon. But I can keep telling myself that's not true.

items.title: Book Review: Broken Money and the Way Out, PART 1: MONEY (the Invity Team)
items.text:
TAKEAWAY NUMERO UNO: If there's a successful book titled *Broken Money*, you DO NOT title your own marketing pamphlet/e-book style "Broken Money" as well.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159635)

***

I spent some time today looking through the Invity people's fintech offering. We met at BTCHEL, where they launched/announced some cool banking features for us Europooreans. https://stacker.news/items/1580878, https://stacker.news/items/1581849 https://stacker.news/items/1585380

Particularly, quite convenient **auto-stacking, payment cards with bitcoin/stablecoins,** and **juicy-af cashback** on every spend. (Up to stupidly [low maximums](https://www.invity.io/personal-accounts), it turns out -.-)

This is all very tempting, and Den is a sucker for a good sats deal (*aren't we all?!*), so what does a bookish nerd do?

## Download and read the free e-book, of course!

***

It's from their educational platform, Invity Academy (as if we didn't have enough educational outlets...):

> It is meant for people who know Bitcoin from headlines and debates, but never got an answer to the most important question: why did it come about at all, and what problem does it solve?
> We start with money itself — how it came about, how it works today, and why so many people feel that something about it „broke“. Only once we understand the problem does it make sense to talk about a solution.

Oh, turns out this is *really* for Mr. Den. Let's dig in.

*Blah-blah-blah*, money's three functions, and various properties (ignoring, for now, Erik Yakes' *7th Property*, **Immutability** https://stacker.news/items/1572208)

![](https://m.stacker.news/159636)

...gold, commodity money, stock-to-flows. Alright, amazing. State intervention, Roman coins.

## "If you were born after 1971, you live in a historical anomaly"

Pretty neat account:

* 1870-1914: Classical gold standard
* 1933: gold banned
* 1971 Nixon Shock

They definitely overdo the importance of 1971, a mere formality in a world already addicted to fiat and money printing. (1914 is a more important civilizational cutoff.)

Cool, but graphs like these are pretty boring. A *dollar*, like *a* bitcoin, is not a meaningful economic unit; nobody (rationally) cares about *a* dollar, but the relationship between what they have and earn to what they invest and consume. e.g., https://stacker.news/items/737272, https://stacker.news/items/1578595

![](https://m.stacker.news/159637)

> 1913 the Fed, 1933 the ban on holding gold, 1944 Bretton Woods, 1971 the Nixon Shock — four steps from hard money to fiat. → Since 1971 no currency in the world has been backed by anything tangible

VERY nice

![](https://m.stacker.news/159638)

> How money is actually created today
> → The vast majority of the money in your account was created by commercial banks, not the state.
> → New money comes into being at the moment of a loan. When you repay the loan, the money disappears.
> → QE lets a central bank create money in the order of trillions within weeks.
> → The M2 money supply grows substantially faster than real output.

## AMAZINGLY witty: "Money-supply inflation is the cause, price inflation is the symptom."

![](https://m.stacker.news/159639)

Here's a scary graph, but of course *financing conditions* matters too: An average interest rate for mortgages in Czechia was about [7% in 2000](https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Average-mortgage-loan-interest-rate-1995-2005_fig7_24080862); [below 5%](https://www.globalpropertyguide.com/europe/czech-republic/mortgage-interest-rate) in 2025.

## Inflation as a silent tax

![](https://m.stacker.news/159641)

> Modern central banking is often defended with the argument that it stimulates the economy and creates jobs. Even if we take that at face value, we must at the same time see the flip side: the money a central bank creates does not arrive for everyone at once. It travels a predictable path that structurally favours one group over another.

VERY eloquent and punchy.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159640)

> At the end of the pipe stand

* **The fixed-wage employee**: the wage is usually adjusted only with a delay, and not by the full extent of inflation.
* **The pensioner** — the pension is indexed once a year, slowly.
* **The young family** without assets — they own no assets to rise in value, yet pay higher prices for food, energy, rent.
  -**The saver** on a savings account — the interest does not cover the loss of purchasing power

These things are conditional and not *obviously* and *always* the case; boomers in America enjoy pretty competitive COLAs; interest rates on savings accounts in Iceland are ~halfway between CPI and monetary expansion. With bond prices collapsing, rates on (high-yield, short-term) bank accounts like those at fintechs are bound to rise explosively. https://stacker.news/items/1578425

***

## NOTHING STOPS THIS LYN ALDEN TRAIN

Yeah, dudes didn't just *borrow* Lyn's title; they take her fiscal framework too: there's no way back/out from governments' profligacy and debt-to-GDP ratios. America just *cannot* outgrow [40trn in debt](https://stacker.news/items/1554591) (...unless we scalp the boomers https://stacker.news/items/1468968, you know the drill.)

> An economic term returning to the debate in recent years is fiscal dominance. It means a state of affairs where the state’s budgetary situation is so strained that the central bank cannot run an independent policy. Lyn Alden describes that the United States entered this situation around 2022. The interest cost on US federal debt exceeded the defence budget in 2024 — and that is a defence budget which is itself larger than the budgets of the next ten largest countries combined.

The financial FIXES that used to work:

* The **60/40 portfolio**: yeah, it's entirely dead. Also, bonds don't provide *neither* uncorrelated returns, nor inflation-adjusted returns at all.
* savings account: guaranteed losses. Czech republic example is \~4% interest on savings, 2.5% official inflation... BUT tax the nominal return 15% *and* assets like flats and properties rose *way more* than 1-2%.
* New fixes?

> Holding large cash in the bank is, over the long run, a strategy by which the state really taxes your purchasing power. Diversification remains valuable, but it must include assets that respond to monetary degradation (hard assets). Gold passed the test of 5,000 years. Neutral, apolitical, independent of the banking system. Bitcoin is new — it has 15 years behind it. But if its properties are confirmed, it offers everything gold does, and more: portability, verifiability, divisibility and neutrality in a form gold can never have.

...in PART 2, dudes move on to the orange solution: \_bitcoin\_, woop woop!

> **If you are a man who cares about climate change, are you a bit of a dweeb? Put another way, if a man says global warming is rubbish, does he seem more manly**? items.title: Why Are Bond Yields Suddenly so High?! (FT, Chris Giles)
items.text:
*Great question, few good answers.*

![](https://m.stacker.news/160553)

"The big question is why yields have risen so much."

* Is it because investors want more compensation for perceived fiscal unsustainability?
* Does it reflect expectations of much faster growth?
* Is there a global war for investment funds and limited lenders?
* Has the Iran war raised the prospect of continued high inflation?
* Is it that central banks signalled the need for persistently higher short-term interest rates and markets are parroting this back?
* Have monetary policymakers lost inflation-fighting credibility?
* Or are bond markets now dominated by flighty hedge funds that can make huge returns if they get a negative narrative to stick?

Chris Giles goes through some of these and provide some decent rebuttals.

> Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said there were [three broad reasons](https://www.federalreserve.gov/mediacenter/files/FOMCpresconf20260916.pdf) at a press conference in September: US economic strength, competition for capital and difficult geopolitics.
> The more important thing he said, however, was that explanations for changes in bond yields “tend to be overdetermined”. In other words, there are many competing but unprovable theories. And he is right.

## "The single clearest cause of the rise in bond yields, as the chart below shows, was President Donald Trump’s decision to initiate war with Iran, before which yields were generally falling"

![](https://m.stacker.news/160554)

Seems obvious, but I'm still a little stuck on the **transmission mechanism** : there's no reason, in principle, that wars or even oil price shocks ought to result in higher yields

The analogy being the 1970 had a few other critical components: **labor unions aggressively striking** for higher wages, setting off a price-wage push; and **central banks eager to accommodate** the real-cost push with new money.

There's no risk for the former, as labor unions worldwide (minus the Nordics, but they're pretty meek here) are a ghost of their former self. And the latter is entirely under our own control; central bankers can decide not to accommodate oil price increases (or actively crush demand... ), thus gaining credibility for their monetary policy *and* an indication of how independent they are from the fiscal authorities.

I guess, then, the bond market is pragmatic and saying "Fat chance, Den; dream the fuck on — dudes will print."

STILL, I find it kind of weird, then, to jump past the intermediate steps and conclude that wars (or oil prices) cause inflation and thus yields.  **No, (central) *banks printing money* cause inflation, *always and everywhere*.** For immediate analogy: Planes don't crash because of gravity, even though of course gravity is involved and 'ultimately' the cause.

> There is no doubt that short-term interest rate expectations have risen across advanced economies. At the start of the year, the Fed was expected to cut rates to almost 3 per cent and now is expected to raise them to 4.75 per cent. That is a huge shift.

Another commonly quipped reason is that AI has unleashed *massive* productivity gains that are about to swamp GDP numbers -- thus rates ought to go up (via the real economy). So far, only a single quarter of a sliver of such indications. AND:

> anyone who remembers 2022, when the US Inflation Reduction Act led to excitement about green growth that did not materialise, should be wary of predicting a massive increase in US growth rates.

Also, this investment boom is not *that* visible (outside specific sectors):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160560)

The other option is that capital is *expensive* now, with AI debt issuance swallowing up all the air in the room, *lol mixing metaphors*:

> Higher yields could simply reflect a massive increase in demand for investible funds that is not met by increased supply. The chart below, which I have borrowed from Toby Nangle’s excellent piece, shows that debt issued by AI hyperscalers accounts for 13.8 per cent of US Treasury issuance, up from only 1.3 per cent in 2024. In other words, there has been a big increase in demand for debt from the AI sector.

> there could still be a general change in the balance between overall debt issuance and debt demand among investors. To the extent that the war for capital is a valid explanation of higher long-term yields, it is more a story of excess debt overall than one to be pinned on the tech bros.

## "No one I have spoken to thinks government debt markets in advanced economies are currently disorderly or signalling impending default."

eeeh, cute. *Maybe look further afield than your standard sources, fren*?!

***

Archive still messing w us... lmk if you want the full article -- lots of good graphs in there.

items.title: Receive-only Lightning checkout: a hacked server can’t drain your node
items.text:
Like a lot of you, we spent August 7 watching merchant Lightning nodes get swept. A bug in BTCPay Server let attackers pull LND macaroons off merchant servers without logging in. With those, they closed channels and walked off with the funds. Foundation, Citadel21, IVPN and others were hit. ([IVPN's writeup](https://www.ivpn.net/blog/security-incident-bitcoin-payment-server/) is worth a read.)

To be clear, we love BTCPay Server. It has done more for merchant adoption than almost anything, and the team responded fast. But that week made something obvious that was always true: keeping a live, spend-capable Lightning node on the same internet-facing machine that runs your shop is fundamentally pretty scary. 

So we built **OpenReceive** to take spending out of the picture entirely.

**How it works**

* Your app connects to your wallet with a **receive-only Nostr Wallet Connect (NWC) code**. That code can create invoices and list incoming payments. It cannot pay anyone.
* On startup, OpenReceive asks the wallet what the code is allowed to do. If the code advertises `pay_invoice` or any other spend method, the app refuses to start.
* There is no send path anywhere in the code.
* Worst case: your server gets owned and the code leaks. The attacker can generate invoices that pay *you* and read your payment history. They can't drain anything. Revoke the code and mint a new one.
* Your node doesn't have to live on the merchant box at all. NWC talks to it over a Nostr relay, so it can sit on separate hardware: Alby Hub, LNbits, or your own CLN node with a zero-budget NWC plugin. Rizful works too if you're small and want something simple.
* No accounts, no API keys, we never touch funds. MIT licensed and self-hosted.

**Works with BTCPay Server, and makes it safer**

You don't have to choose. There's an OpenReceive plugin in the BTCPay plugin directory (BTCPay 2.4.4+). Paste in a receive-only NWC code and your wallet becomes the store's Lightning node. BTCPay keeps doing what it's good at, including invoices, accounting, and the Woo/Odoo/Magento/PrestaShop integrations. The difference is that there's no node with spendable macaroons sitting on the server anymore. The tradeoff, by design: no Lightning payouts or refunds from that backend.

If you're not on BTCPay, there are drop-in libraries for Express, Fastify, Next.js, NestJS, FastAPI, Django, Flask, Rails, PHP/Laravel, plus a WooCommerce plugin.

**Yes, about the stablecoins…**

OpenReceive can *optionally* accept USDT and USDC (also SOL and ETH) through a swap provider you configure. The payment is swapped automatically to BTC over Lightning and settles in your wallet. The merchant never holds a stablecoin. They receive sats.

We did this because the reality is a lot of people want to pay with this. In a lot of the world, dollar stablecoins are how people actually hold and move money. We think the best way to bring Bitcoin adoption to those people is to have the merchants actually receive Lightning. Every one of those payments ends up as a bitcoin buy, and every merchant who turns it on is running a Lightning checkout.

If you don't want it, don't turn it on. Swaps are off unless you add a provider. One honest caveat: swaps add complexity, because a short or late deposit has to be refunded on the payer's chain. That flow is documented.

**Links**

* Docs: [https://openreceive.org](https://openreceive.org)
* BTCPay plugin: [https://openreceive.org/btcpay](https://openreceive.org/btcpay)
* Source: [https://github.com/OpenReceive/openreceive](https://github.com/OpenReceive/openreceive)

We'd genuinely love for this crowd to try to break it. Tell us what we got wrong.

items.title: New motherhood level unlocked
items.text:
I am feeling something I haven't felt in a very long time. When my daughter was born, the first month was a strange transition from being an individual with no serious responsibilities to a first-time mom. Adapting takes time. Just when I reached the peak of motherhood knowledge (or so I thought), a new level would unlock and I’d have to start from scratch—understanding new sleep routines, learning the different decibels of her crying, new sounds, skills, and needs. I felt lost at first from not understanding and having to wing it just to do a halfway decent or acceptable job, feeling frustrated for not measuring up to what is expected or what "should be." This happened to me every month during my daughter's first year, which is normal because children experience accelerated physical and mental growth during their first two years. The last time I was in this situation was about 6 or 7 years ago (my daughter is now 9).

I write these words with a lot of nostalgia in my heart. Once again, I feel in limbo, lost, without clarity; everything looks blurry. This level is the hardest one I’ve played so far, and I am well aware that it gets even more complicated down the road—anyone with adult children or teenagers can attest to that.

The window has now opened to seek psychological support; nothing severe, but definitely necessary. The dilemma of unwanted friendships... this moment is the preamble to review and analyze the parenting you’ve done, your skills as a parent, and the phase where you can still fix certain patterns you've instilled, reinforce what you've done well, change what doesn't work, and improve. I feel so much tension, pressure, and stress—it’s like I’m running somewhere and can’t find the finish line. Whether you speak, act, or react one way or another, it seems like it will cause some trauma or similar bullshit in your kids anyway. If you scold them, raise your voice, use the wrong adjective, if you were too soft, if you were strict, if you spoiled them, supported them or didn't—it doesn't matter, it's all the same, you caused a trauma. Tantrums are no longer about your child throwing themselves on the floor because they want to eat from the blue plate and you served it on the green one. Now, tantrums, tolerance levels, empathy, and respect are seen when they socialize with their friends. Teaching the art of patience, communication, and boundaries is a challenge; you’re supposed to have been doing it for years, but they start acting differently—they imitate you and they imitate their friends. This stage defines the type of attachment style they will have in adulthood, among countless other events. Of course, I am speaking from my own experience, because every life, child, and person is different. And right now, I am on the edge—questioning, analyzing, and thinking about how to surf this level. In the end, the hard part isn't raising a child; the hard part is educating ourselves, unlearning and learning, and giving to ourselves while we raise a little person.

> At age 9, children enter what the Child Mind Institute describes as a metacognitive state. This means that:
> 
> Self-awareness ("The Self"): They leave behind the concrete thinking of childhood to develop abstract and critical thinking. For the first time, they realize they are completely separate individuals from their parents, which generates a mix of melancholy and insecurity due to losing the protection of early childhood.
> 
> The fall of the "Perfect Parents": Scientifically, it is observed that at this age, their perception toward their parents changes. They no longer see you as an infallible being, but as a human. That is why they question you, imitate you, and test your reactions.

items.title: My daughter gave me money
items.text:
My daughter asked me to take her wallet from the drawer. For some inexplicable reason, she took out $2 from her wallet and passed it to me.

“I want to give it to you!” she insisted.

So, I pocketed her $2 without hesitation. (I would transfer $2 to her bank account subsequently.) Young children can be so sweet. Giving of themselves unconditionally without really expecting anything in return . It was good to know that she has my back. Hopefully, she will retain this generosity of spirit as she grows up.

Bitcoin is Worth It - Being Hard

Its 7am on a Saturday as I write this.

No. AI is not being used here.

Bitcoin just completed another cycle.

And in dollar terms it was the least volatile.Up and down. The run up multiple to the ATH, and the bear down was tame this time around. Less euphoria, less destruction. At least in the market metrics.

In terms of Bitcoins social aspect though, the destruction was and is acutely poignant, reminiscent of the blocksize wars drama. Enough time has gone by to take stalk of some of this damage objectively. This is an attempt in that, with a hopeful path forward through the noise.

Beginning with the damage.

A group of node maxis were ultimately deceived into forking off for religiously ideological logic. this was a loss of a praetorian guard like unit that patrolled the capital maintaining order and good Bitcoin common sense, such as running a node, and understanding the why of doing so. Meanwhile the bitcoin dev priesthood gets high off estrogen and its own flatulence that it calls inspired hot air, with the same communist double speak it used to gaslight its tenth man into self imposed exile. The social sludge that surrounds that whole affair has also further weakened bonds between peers. Many have broken.Bad faith returning bad faith.Tit for tat making us blind and more isolated in our scattered digital conclaves.Which can be healthy.

Tolerating evil enables it.Saving your time and strength on non swine protects your pearls. With that said, burnout is endemic. A libatious holiday is needed by all.Go to your local spas folks.Get that message. The fight isn't over and you're rest, health and sound mind are needed to confront the dark of an uncertain future that needs your light.

Back to the damage assessment.What is the lesson of that food fight in the dev cafeteria?

Devs are human, and are thus just as retarded as the rest of us.They will in many cases act out of their own self interested political machinations, and argue in bad faith to achieve those aims without regard for decent logic.They turn that off as a ends-justify-the-means tactic to avoid discussing their real logic, which can be disturbingly greedy,partisan, culture-war-retarded, and evil.Or at least lacking a moral compass that points in one direction. Communist rhetoric playbook embodied. So devs really cant be trusted. Especially if they're generating your bitcoin keys for you.

In prior cycles the not-your-keys-not-your-bitcoin lesson emerged from mtgox, and was reinforced by echoing blowups of trusted third parties, like ftx. A hard lesson at first, but redundant in 2020 and easily tolerated.It was harder this time around to learn that bitcoin only hardware wallets are also trusted third parties, though not obvious ones.

Self custody is Bitcoin. and like Bitcoin, self custody is hard. the coldcard entropy bug is a lesson in that.We've collectively been trusting these devices to generate a large random number to secure our Bitcoin, when we need not to.We can and should roll dice, flip a lot of coins or do any number of other truly random activities to generate the master secret to our elliptic curve vault. We can and should verify ourselves. Hard collective lesson. Worth learning.Probably a good time to learn it too.And being learned by the ones who can learn it.The bitcoin maxi crowd were argent coldcard users. This current pain,too, shall pass.Like MTGOX. But, Don’t Forget.

Pathos comes to mind.Hubris and pride always before the fall.Mea culpa wont fix this, but its the necessary path forward by ritualistic law.Take the L. Live to fight another day.

Onward now to an apology.Those who know know.Sorry if you don't get it.Many of you will.

So Bitcoin is learning some more hard lessons.Trusted third parties are blowing up in new and shitty ways.Socially its frayed. needs a vacation, some mea culpa tea and a warm blanket. But all of this is within tolerance levels, echoes of past events too. Perhaps growing pains is an apt description. New necessary mass casualty events as instructive lessons in verification?

On the eve of Bitcoins 18th, Bitcoin finds itself larger then ever before as a collective. But also older. That youthful innocent energy is no longer there.Now we have something to lose, more then gain.The rose-orange tinted glasses of a bitcoin community have faded.People reverting to their natural state as assholes.

Naturally infighting happens in any group larger then 100. And Bitcoin has many 100s of thousands of users.Less peers now though.More enemies.

But, chronic fiat inflation, endless wars, an oil supply shock, nuclear scares and an AI powered future will probably paper over all this damage.Time heals all wounds, and Bitcoin is Time. Bitcoin blocks tick tock, the world continues to eat itself, and value climbs to the worthy high ground on the hard rock in cyberspace.

The self perpetuating cycle continues so long as Bitcoin remains hard and fiat easy.IF true then statement fulfilled.Activating cycle bottom.

Learn the hard lesson. Never stop Verifying all the way up and down.

Bitcoin is Worth being hard.And it’s Worth Everything Because it is Hard.

If you respect and put in the hard work of Bitcoin and take care of it by verifying, it will take care of you.If you trust, take shortcuts, make excuses, don't put in the proof of work to verify, natural selection will activate, eventually to humble you. Murphy’s law applies. Bitcoin isn’t a concrete fiat dystopia here to serve slop for your baser prideful needs.Its a digital jungle with giant lurking cats with snakes in the grass.Survival is the imperative.If you survive,you'll thrive.You survive by verifying.Use the scientific method of double checking and replicating results.

Don't get complacent, there's always another bear around the corner looking for your bitcoin honey.

the jungles only going to get wilder, so buckle down, get hard, verify.

Don't trust the devs, don't trust your hardware wallets, put in the hard work to verify.If you do, bitcoin will take care of you.

Bitcoin is Worth It.

items.title: The Genesis Code, Ch. 8: Vital Signs
items.text:
*Harold*

"It doesn't have blood," Toshi said, for the fourth time.

"I heard you the first three."

"I'm saying it again because I want you to *understand* it, Harold. It has no blood. It has no heart. It has a pump that circulates coolant, and the coolant is blue, and it smells like a new shower curtain." He was pacing the storage unit in tight little circles, the way he used to pace the back of the art room when a sculpture wasn't drying fast enough. "They're going to stick a needle in its arm, and what's going to come out is Windex."

Noah sat in his camping chair with his hands folded, looking pleasant. He had no opinion on the matter.

The invitation from Cyrus Vail lay open on the little folding table between us. Heavy cream paper, gold edges, a wax seal like an open book. Inside, in handwriting so elegant it looked engraved, was an address in Cincinnati, a date, and a line at the bottom that Toshi had read aloud in a voice of mounting horror:

*A brief physical examination will precede your welcome. Our physician is very thorough.*

"What does the unit have?" I asked. "On the outside. What will pass?"

Toshi stopped pacing. He counted on his fingers.

"Skin temperature, yes. It runs warm. Ninety-eight point four at the surface. Pulse at the wrist, yes, sort of. There's a little actuator there, for handshakes, so it feels alive. It breathes if you tell it to. Blinks, sweats a little under lights. It can pass a doctor who shakes its hand and asks about its golf game." He dropped his hand. "It cannot pass a stethoscope. It cannot pass an EKG. And it absolutely cannot pass a blood draw."

"Then we don't go."

"If we don't go, the most powerful people in America want to know why their candidate won't let a doctor touch him."

"Then we say he's sick."

"Then they send *their* doctor to *him*."

I rubbed my eyes. The shaved patch on the back of my head itched. It always itched when I thought too hard, as if the implant were thinking too.

"The man in the hangar warned us," I said slowly. "Vail. He said *I'd prepare for that, if I were you.* Why warn us if he wanted us caught?"

"Maybe he wants to watch us sweat."

"Robots don't sweat, Toshi."

"*A little.* Under lights." He sat down hard on the concrete floor with his back against the wall. "I don't know what he wants. I don't know what anyone wants. I used to fix torque curves in hip joints."

We sat there a while. Outside, a truck went by on the county road, and the orange door rattled in its track.

"We go," I said finally.

Toshi looked up.

"We go," I said again. "Because if we don't, it's over anyway. And because a man who meant us harm wouldn't have warned us. And because—" I stopped.

"Because what?"

I looked at Noah, sitting there with his hands folded and his eyes closed.

"Because I have a feeling," I said, "that we're not the only ones who need this to work."

\* \* \*

The address was a townhouse in Cincinnati, three stories of red brick on a quiet street full of trees older than the country. A brass plate by the door said PRIVATE PRACTICE, and nothing else. The black sedan dropped Noah at the curb at 9:00 a.m. sharp, and he climbed the steps with the easy, loose-shouldered confidence of a man who had never once in his life been kept waiting.

In a storage unit in Paperton, two hundred and fifty miles north, I sat in a green camping chair with a blanket over my knees and a bucket beside me, in case the nerves came out the wrong way.

"Heart rate's a hundred and twelve," Toshi said, from the next room of my mind. "Your real one."

"Stop telling me that."

"It's my job."

"It's making it worse."

"Okay." A pause. "It's a hundred and fifteen now."

\* \* \*

The waiting room was paneled in dark wood, with oil portraits of men in high collars who all seemed to have been painted in the same mood. There was one other person there, a woman in a nurse's scrubs sitting at a small desk with a clipboard. She didn't look like a nurse. She looked like someone who'd been told to sit in a room and watch the door, and who was very good at it.

"Mr. Fiatt," she said. "The doctor will be right with you."

Noah sat. I made him cross one leg over the other and look at his watch, because that's what important men do in waiting rooms. The watch said 9:04. I watched the second hand go around, and around, and I thought about all the drawings I'd done of clocks in my life, and how the hands always want to look like they're pointing somewhere.

At 9:09 an inner door opened.

I'd expected an old man. Some courtly society physician with a silver mustache, a pocket watch, a leather bag that had belonged to his grandfather. What came through the door was a woman in her forties, brisk and plain, in a white coat with her hair pulled back, carrying a tablet.

"Mr. Fiatt," she said. "I'm Dr. Veritas. Dr. Penrose is unwell this morning, so I'm covering. I hope that's all right."

The nurse at the desk looked up sharply. For just a second her face did something complicated. Then she looked down at her clipboard again.

"Of course," I said, in Noah's warm gravel voice.

As Dr. Veritas turned to lead us in, I caught a glimpse of the lanyard around her neck. It was tucked mostly inside her coat. But the clip was showing, and on the clip was a tiny logo I'd last seen on the Mindlink letter at my kitchen table, and on the wall of a clinic that used to be an Applebee's.

A little brain made of glowing dots, holding hands with itself.

"Toshi," I said silently. "Look at her lanyard."

There was a pause in my head.

"That's Mindlink," he said.

\* \* \*

The exam room was bright and white and very cold. Dr. Veritas had me sit on the paper-covered table and take off Noah's jacket and shirt, and I did it slowly, carefully, the way you undress in front of a stranger, and I felt more naked than I'd ever felt in my own body. Noah's chest was perfect. Smooth, tan, lightly haired, with a small scar on the left shoulder that Proxy had added, Toshi told me later, because a man without a single scar makes people nervous.

The nurse from the waiting room came in and stood by the door with her clipboard. Nobody had asked her to.

"Deep breath," said Dr. Veritas, and put the stethoscope on Noah's chest.

I made him breathe. In, out. In, out. Under the cold disc of the stethoscope there was nothing. No heart. Just the soft, steady whir of a coolant pump, turning like a ceiling fan in an empty house.

Dr. Veritas listened for a long time.

In Paperton, my real heart was going like a hammer on a tin roof. I could feel it through the connection. I could feel both at once, my racket and Noah's hush, and the gap between them was the most frightening sound I'd ever heard.

The nurse at the door leaned slightly forward.

Dr. Veritas moved the stethoscope an inch to the left. Listened again. Then she took it out of her ears, looped it around her neck, and made a note on her tablet.

"Strong heart," she said. "Very regular."

The nurse leaned back again.

I didn't breathe. Noah did, because I'd forgotten to tell him to stop.

\* \* \*

The EKG came next. Dr. Veritas stuck little white pads to Noah's chest and wrists and ankles, and clipped wires to them, and the wires ran to a small gray machine on a cart. Except I was watching, the way I'd learned to watch in thirty-one years of kids hiding phones under their desks, and I saw where the wires went. They didn't go to the machine. They went into the machine's side panel and came right back out again, bundled under the cart, to the tablet in her hand.

The screen on the cart lit up. A green line began to march across it. Up, down, spike, dip. Up, down, spike, dip. A perfect, healthy, middle-aged American heartbeat, beating for a man who had no heart at all.

"Beautiful," said Dr. Veritas, not looking at it.

Then she picked up the needle.

"Just a small pinch," she said.

Toshi said something in my head that I won't repeat.

She tied the rubber band around Noah's arm, swabbed the inside of his elbow with alcohol, and turned slightly on her stool, so that for just a moment her back was to the nurse at the door. It was a small movement. The kind a magician makes. If I hadn't spent three decades watching children try to palm erasers, I would never have seen it.

The needle went into the arm. I felt it the way you feel a pinch through a thick coat, far away and unimportant.

The vial on the end of the needle filled with blood.

Dark red. Real. Swirling.

I stared at it through Noah's eyes, and for one dizzy second I genuinely did not know what I was looking at. Then I saw it: the vial had been full before it touched him. There'd been a second one in her palm the whole time. The one that had actually gone into the arm was in her coat pocket now, and whatever was in it was blue and smelled like a new shower curtain.

She capped the full vial, labeled it, and handed it over her shoulder to the nurse without looking.

"For the lab," she said.

The nurse took it. She held it up to the light. She looked at it for a long moment.

Then she wrote something on her clipboard, and left the room.

\* \* \*

"You're in excellent health, Mr. Fiatt," said Dr. Veritas, pulling off the pads one by one. "Better than most men your age. Better than most men half your age." She peeled the last one from his ankle. "Keep doing whatever you're doing."

I put Noah's shirt back on. My fingers, his fingers, fumbled a little on the buttons. She noticed. She didn't say anything.

She walked me to the inner door. With her hand on the knob, she paused, and without turning her head, she spoke, very quietly, in the voice people use when they're talking to someone who isn't in the room.

"Mindlink sends its regards."

I said nothing. I wasn't sure Noah's mouth still worked.

"And tell him," she said, even more quietly, "that the headaches are dehydration. Most of our older participants don't drink enough water after the procedure. Eight glasses a day."

She opened the door.

"Have a wonderful day, Mr. Fiatt."

\* \* \*

The sedan brought Noah back to Paperton at two in the afternoon. By then I'd already let go, somewhere around Dayton, because my hands had started shaking so badly Toshi was afraid it would bleed through the connection. I sat in the camping chair with the blanket around my shoulders and drank a whole bottle of water in one long pull, and then I started laughing, and then I stopped.

"They know," Toshi said. He hadn't sat down since nine. "Mindlink knows. They know it's you. They know about the implant. They know about the robot. They sent their own doctor, Harold. They got rid of the real one."

"I know."

"They could have ended us in that room. One word to that nurse. One." He turned in a tight circle. "Why didn't they?"

I looked across at Noah in his chair, eyes closed, hands folded. Somewhere inside him was a line of code nobody could read, and somewhere inside me was a chip made by a company whose partners owned every thought I'd had since March.

I thought about page thirty-eight of the consent form. *Mindlink Labs and its partners.* I thought about how Toshi's cable had plugged into Noah so easily, *almost like somebody designed them to fit together*.

I thought about a vial of blue coolant, sitting in the pocket of a Mindlink doctor's coat, that could bring down a great deal more than one old man in Paperton.

"Because they can't," I said.

Toshi stopped circling.

"If they expose Noah," I said, working it out as I went, "somebody asks what Noah is. And then somebody asks who else is one. And whatever Mindlink's part in that is, it goes on the front page too." I set the empty bottle down on the concrete. "We're not the only ones hiding something in this room, Toshi. We're just the only ones who didn't know it."

The storage unit was quiet. Outside, the Dollar Depot sign buzzed. DOLL R DEP.

After a while, Toshi went to the cooler and got me another bottle of water. He set it down next to my chair without a word.

I drank it. Eight glasses a day. Doctor's orders.

---

items.title: I finally visited Pubkey in Washington DC
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/162019)

I am attending a reunion of sorts of some old friends in DC.  I had some free time yesterday, so I finally got the opportunity to visit the Washington Pubkey.

I have posted a few times about the NYC version. I have a great time whenever I go:

https://stacker.news/items/219987/r/siggy47

https://stacker.news/items/230440/r/siggy47

https://stacker.news/items/1283387/r/siggy47

The Washington DC version of Pubkey is located on 7th Street in the [Penn Quarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Quarter) neighborhood of the city. It's not far from Ford's Theater and the J Edgar Hoover FBI building.  Capital One Arena, where the Washington Capitals play, is down the block. It is an upscale, touristy location.

Pubkey DC opened in January, 2026, according to the website, but I thought it had been around longer.  Yesterday the Washington Capitals had an early game, so there were plenty of fans in jerseys milling about. When I walked in I immediately noticed how different this place was from the New York version. It's huge, around 12,000 square feet, with two bars, a stage, and big screens everywhere showing sporting events. There was a good crowd, which looked to be a mix of tourists, locals, and hockey fans. I can't be certain, but I'm pretty sure I was the only person in the place interested in bitcoin.

This is not an in your face bitcoin space. I had just had a long car and was hungry. I decided to sit at the bar and have some lunch after exploring a bit.

At first I didn't notice much bitcoin stuff, but it is all strategically placed to fit in unobtrusively. I liked the low key design. It could be any sports /tourist spot in any city.

There were a few stickers in the men's room:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162028)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162029)

I then noticed a large wall display with some actively mining bitaxes:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162030)

And this small, but intriguing stack of bitcoin and bitcoin adjacent books below a "Free Samourai" sign:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162032)

I sat at the bar and saw this cool display:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162033)

Occasionally the ticker had a news flash scrolling across the screen.

When ordering my lunch I let the bartender know that I planned to pay in bitcoin. I was told that if I did, I would receive a 21% discount, which is impressive. I asked about the payment setup, and was a little disappointed that they just use square. I tried to.engage my server in a little bitcoin banter, but it was obvious he had no deep interest. I dont want to sound negative. All of the workers were friendly and competent. The menu was similar to the NYC Pubkey. I had a Caesar wrap, which was very good.  I must say paying with the square app was quick and easy. You select the tip amount before the invoice is generated, which is nice. I have experienced a few awkward moments trying to tip at the NYC Pubkey. You never can be sure if the server would prefer sats or dollars. This way they probably get a choice.

That being said, paying with square is still disappointing.

On the way out I found this board near the front bar:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162036)

I guess this proves there are some bitcoiners patronizing the place.

I didn't get to experience an event, but there is plenty of room for bitcoin gatherings. NYC Pubkey always feels a little cramped. I know Thomas Massie will be holding a discussion soon. I hope I get some time on my next trip to catch a presentation.

> **Escaping Venezuela lays bare the human cost of the socialist project.**
>
> The documentary [Escaping Venezuela](https://escapingvenezuela.reason.com/) portrays the unprecedented unfolding of the contemporary Venezuelan crisis, one that cannot be grasped through constitutional, political science, international law, or electoral analysis alone. Its present dimensions are rooted in a broader historical arc spanning 1958 to 2026. That arc began with a functioning, peaceful yet imperfect democracy in what was then one of Latin America’s wealthiest nations (1958–1999). It gave way to twenty-first-century socialism under Hugo Chávez (1999–2013) and Nicolás Maduro (2013–2026), an era defined by institutional decay, the dismantling of democracy, the capture of state institutions by criminal networks with international ties, profound economic and social collapse, and systematic human rights violations. It now enters a new phase marked by the Trump administration’s asserted control over Venezuela, following the January 3, 2026, military operation that seized Nicolás Maduro, whom much of the international community regarded as a usurper, and brought him before the United States (U.S.) federal courts. 
>
> At the beginning of Venezuela’s democratic era, the system relied on consensus among the major political parties on key issues. It also gradually incorporated national business organizations, labor unions, and religious groups into a semi-corporatist framework that allowed them to participate in key economic and political decisions. Over time, the bipartisan system evolved into a complex, conflict-ridden multiparty system, with organizations outside the parties becoming increasingly influential. This convergence of diverse, competing interests, along with the risk these groups perceived to their sometimes-opaque privileges and interests from the market-friendly economic reforms of the late 1980s, weakened democracy and enabled practices that undermined economic and political integrity.  
>
> The documentary vividly describes how during the second presidency of social democrat Carlos Andrés Pérez (1989–1993), Venezuela was shaken by the *Caracazo,* a wave of protests, riots, and looting that began on February 27, 1989. Amnesty International reported that human rights organizations identified approximately 400 people who died or went missing during the events. Some commentators contend that the *Caracazo* was planned rather than entirely spontaneous. They cite reports that politically active students occupied public transportation facilities at 6 a.m. on February 27, 1989, and distributed preprinted leaflets. They also point to allegations that police had been instructed not to intervene, while President Carlos Andrés Pérez blamed police insubordination. Some accounts cite evidence of coordination and identify Jorge Rodríguez, then a student leader and later a prominent figure in Venezuela’s socialist government, as an organizer. Paulina Gamus, who chaired the congressional inquiry, believed the unrest had been orchestrated but had spiraled out of control. Chávez later said the *Caracazo* helped spur his plans for the 1992 coup attempt.

items.title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
items.text:
> **Moritz Hardt, author of a new book on benchmarks, believes these “standardized tests” for artificial intelligence are fundamentally broken — but not unfixable.**
>
> Benchmarks are the rulers of AI, in both senses of the word. As measuring sticks, they work according to an extremely simple logic: If you want to know what an AI model can do, devise a standardized test to gauge it. But AI benchmarks can also dominate the behavior of the entire field.
>
> In 1987, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s [first benchmark](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.06647v1#S5) on automatic speech-to-text translation showed that state-of-the-art AI could not outperform so-called “dumb” statistical approaches. The poor performance helped to usher in an AI winter. For 25 years, interest in AI research waned and funding dried up.
>
> Then, in 2012, [another benchmark](https://www.image-net.org/challenges/LSVRC/index.php) called ImageNet swung the pendulum back. An eight-layer neural network [trounced](https://spectrum.ieee.org/alexnet-source-code) other algorithms at classifying images and kicked off a “deep learning revolution.”
>
> Nowadays, new AI benchmarks, geared at large language models such as OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, get created and solved with clockwork regularity, purporting to measure everything from [domain-specific expertise](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report/technical-performance) to “[general intelligence](https://arcprize.org/arc-agi).” But rather than hail this trend as proof of AI’s skyrocketing potential, many in the field — [skeptics](https://x.com/GaryMarcus/status/2028488127875342724) and [boosters](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1896266683301659068?lang=en) alike — take it as evidence that benchmarking itself has become [fatally flawed](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-02462-5).

items.title: Receive-only Lightning checkout: a hacked server can’t drain your node
items.text:
Like a lot of you, we spent August 7 watching merchant Lightning nodes get swept. A bug in BTCPay Server let attackers pull LND macaroons off merchant servers without logging in. With those, they closed channels and walked off with the funds. Foundation, Citadel21, IVPN and others were hit. ([IVPN's writeup](https://www.ivpn.net/blog/security-incident-bitcoin-payment-server/) is worth a read.)

To be clear, we love BTCPay Server. It has done more for merchant adoption than almost anything, and the team responded fast. But that week made something obvious that was always true: keeping a live, spend-capable Lightning node on the same internet-facing machine that runs your shop is fundamentally pretty scary. 

So we built **OpenReceive** to take spending out of the picture entirely.

**How it works**

* Your app connects to your wallet with a **receive-only Nostr Wallet Connect (NWC) code**. That code can create invoices and list incoming payments. It cannot pay anyone.
* On startup, OpenReceive asks the wallet what the code is allowed to do. If the code advertises `pay_invoice` or any other spend method, the app refuses to start.
* There is no send path anywhere in the code.
* Worst case: your server gets owned and the code leaks. The attacker can generate invoices that pay *you* and read your payment history. They can't drain anything. Revoke the code and mint a new one.
* Your node doesn't have to live on the merchant box at all. NWC talks to it over a Nostr relay, so it can sit on separate hardware: Alby Hub, LNbits, or your own CLN node with a zero-budget NWC plugin. Rizful works too if you're small and want something simple.
* No accounts, no API keys, we never touch funds. MIT licensed and self-hosted.

**Works with BTCPay Server, and makes it safer**

You don't have to choose. There's an OpenReceive plugin in the BTCPay plugin directory (BTCPay 2.4.4+). Paste in a receive-only NWC code and your wallet becomes the store's Lightning node. BTCPay keeps doing what it's good at, including invoices, accounting, and the Woo/Odoo/Magento/PrestaShop integrations. The difference is that there's no node with spendable macaroons sitting on the server anymore. The tradeoff, by design: no Lightning payouts or refunds from that backend.

If you're not on BTCPay, there are drop-in libraries for Express, Fastify, Next.js, NestJS, FastAPI, Django, Flask, Rails, PHP/Laravel, plus a WooCommerce plugin.

**Yes, about the stablecoins…**

OpenReceive can *optionally* accept USDT and USDC (also SOL and ETH) through a swap provider you configure. The payment is swapped automatically to BTC over Lightning and settles in your wallet. The merchant never holds a stablecoin. They receive sats.

We did this because the reality is a lot of people want to pay with this. In a lot of the world, dollar stablecoins are how people actually hold and move money. We think the best way to bring Bitcoin adoption to those people is to have the merchants actually receive Lightning. Every one of those payments ends up as a bitcoin buy, and every merchant who turns it on is running a Lightning checkout.

If you don't want it, don't turn it on. Swaps are off unless you add a provider. One honest caveat: swaps add complexity, because a short or late deposit has to be refunded on the payer's chain. That flow is documented.

**Links**

* Docs: [https://openreceive.org](https://openreceive.org)
* BTCPay plugin: [https://openreceive.org/btcpay](https://openreceive.org/btcpay)
* Source: [https://github.com/OpenReceive/openreceive](https://github.com/OpenReceive/openreceive)

We'd genuinely love for this crowd to try to break it. Tell us what we got wrong.

items.title: New motherhood level unlocked
items.text:
I am feeling something I haven't felt in a very long time. When my daughter was born, the first month was a strange transition from being an individual with no serious responsibilities to a first-time mom. Adapting takes time. Just when I reached the peak of motherhood knowledge (or so I thought), a new level would unlock and I’d have to start from scratch—understanding new sleep routines, learning the different decibels of her crying, new sounds, skills, and needs. I felt lost at first from not understanding and having to wing it just to do a halfway decent or acceptable job, feeling frustrated for not measuring up to what is expected or what "should be." This happened to me every month during my daughter's first year, which is normal because children experience accelerated physical and mental growth during their first two years. The last time I was in this situation was about 6 or 7 years ago (my daughter is now 9).

I write these words with a lot of nostalgia in my heart. Once again, I feel in limbo, lost, without clarity; everything looks blurry. This level is the hardest one I’ve played so far, and I am well aware that it gets even more complicated down the road—anyone with adult children or teenagers can attest to that.

The window has now opened to seek psychological support; nothing severe, but definitely necessary. The dilemma of unwanted friendships... this moment is the preamble to review and analyze the parenting you’ve done, your skills as a parent, and the phase where you can still fix certain patterns you've instilled, reinforce what you've done well, change what doesn't work, and improve. I feel so much tension, pressure, and stress—it’s like I’m running somewhere and can’t find the finish line. Whether you speak, act, or react one way or another, it seems like it will cause some trauma or similar bullshit in your kids anyway. If you scold them, raise your voice, use the wrong adjective, if you were too soft, if you were strict, if you spoiled them, supported them or didn't—it doesn't matter, it's all the same, you caused a trauma. Tantrums are no longer about your child throwing themselves on the floor because they want to eat from the blue plate and you served it on the green one. Now, tantrums, tolerance levels, empathy, and respect are seen when they socialize with their friends. Teaching the art of patience, communication, and boundaries is a challenge; you’re supposed to have been doing it for years, but they start acting differently—they imitate you and they imitate their friends. This stage defines the type of attachment style they will have in adulthood, among countless other events. Of course, I am speaking from my own experience, because every life, child, and person is different. And right now, I am on the edge—questioning, analyzing, and thinking about how to surf this level. In the end, the hard part isn't raising a child; the hard part is educating ourselves, unlearning and learning, and giving to ourselves while we raise a little person.

> At age 9, children enter what the Child Mind Institute describes as a metacognitive state. This means that:
> 
> Self-awareness ("The Self"): They leave behind the concrete thinking of childhood to develop abstract and critical thinking. For the first time, they realize they are completely separate individuals from their parents, which generates a mix of melancholy and insecurity due to losing the protection of early childhood.
> 
> The fall of the "Perfect Parents": Scientifically, it is observed that at this age, their perception toward their parents changes. They no longer see you as an infallible being, but as a human. That is why they question you, imitate you, and test your reactions.

Self custody is Bitcoin. and like Bitcoin, self custody is hard. the coldcard entropy bug is a lesson in that.We've collectively been trusting these devices to generate a large random number to secure our Bitcoin, when we need not to.We can and should roll dice, flip a lot of coins or do any number of other truly random activities to generate the master secret to our elliptic curve vault. We can and should verify ourselves. Hard collective lesson. Worth learning.Probably a good time to learn it too.And being learned by the ones who can learn it.The bitcoin maxi crowd were argent coldcard users. This current pain,too, shall pass.Like MTGOX. But, Don’t Forget.

Pathos comes to mind.Hubris and pride always before the fall.Mea culpa wont fix this, but its the necessary path forward by ritualistic law.Take the L. Live to fight another day.

Onward now to an apology.Those who know know.Sorry if you don't get it.Many of you will.

So Bitcoin is learning some more hard lessons.Trusted third parties are blowing up in new and shitty ways.Socially its frayed. needs a vacation, some mea culpa tea and a warm blanket. But all of this is within tolerance levels, echoes of past events too. Perhaps growing pains is an apt description. New necessary mass casualty events as instructive lessons in verification?

On the eve of Bitcoins 18th, Bitcoin finds itself larger then ever before as a collective. But also older. That youthful innocent energy is no longer there.Now we have something to lose, more then gain.The rose-orange tinted glasses of a bitcoin community have faded.People reverting to their natural state as assholes.

Naturally infighting happens in any group larger then 100. And Bitcoin has many 100s of thousands of users.Less peers now though.More enemies.

But, chronic fiat inflation, endless wars, an oil supply shock, nuclear scares and an AI powered future will probably paper over all this damage.Time heals all wounds, and Bitcoin is Time. Bitcoin blocks tick tock, the world continues to eat itself, and value climbs to the worthy high ground on the hard rock in cyberspace.

The self perpetuating cycle continues so long as Bitcoin remains hard and fiat easy.IF true then statement fulfilled.Activating cycle bottom.

Learn the hard lesson. Never stop Verifying all the way up and down.

Bitcoin is Worth being hard.And it’s Worth Everything Because it is Hard.

If you respect and put in the hard work of Bitcoin and take care of it by verifying, it will take care of you.If you trust, take shortcuts, make excuses, don't put in the proof of work to verify, natural selection will activate, eventually to humble you. Murphy’s law applies. Bitcoin isn’t a concrete fiat dystopia here to serve slop for your baser prideful needs.Its a digital jungle with giant lurking cats with snakes in the grass.Survival is the imperative.If you survive,you'll thrive.You survive by verifying.Use the scientific method of double checking and replicating results.

Don't get complacent, there's always another bear around the corner looking for your bitcoin honey.

the jungles only going to get wilder, so buckle down, get hard, verify.
