items.text:
*Harold*

"It doesn't have blood," Toshi said, for the fourth time.

"I heard you the first three."

"I'm saying it again because I want you to *understand* it, Harold. It has no blood. It has no heart. It has a pump that circulates coolant, and the coolant is blue, and it smells like a new shower curtain." He was pacing the storage unit in tight little circles, the way he used to pace the back of the art room when a sculpture wasn't drying fast enough. "They're going to stick a needle in its arm, and what's going to come out is Windex."

Noah sat in his camping chair with his hands folded, looking pleasant. He had no opinion on the matter.

The invitation from Cyrus Vail lay open on the little folding table between us. Heavy cream paper, gold edges, a wax seal like an open book. Inside, in handwriting so elegant it looked engraved, was an address in Cincinnati, a date, and a line at the bottom that Toshi had read aloud in a voice of mounting horror:

*A brief physical examination will precede your welcome. Our physician is very thorough.*

"What does the unit have?" I asked. "On the outside. What will pass?"

Toshi stopped pacing. He counted on his fingers.

"Skin temperature, yes. It runs warm. Ninety-eight point four at the surface. Pulse at the wrist, yes, sort of. There's a little actuator there, for handshakes, so it feels alive. It breathes if you tell it to. Blinks, sweats a little under lights. It can pass a doctor who shakes its hand and asks about its golf game." He dropped his hand. "It cannot pass a stethoscope. It cannot pass an EKG. And it absolutely cannot pass a blood draw."

"Then we don't go."

"If we don't go, the most powerful people in America want to know why their candidate won't let a doctor touch him."

"Then we say he's sick."

"Then they send *their* doctor to *him*."

I rubbed my eyes. The shaved patch on the back of my head itched. It always itched when I thought too hard, as if the implant were thinking too.

"The man in the hangar warned us," I said slowly. "Vail. He said *I'd prepare for that, if I were you.* Why warn us if he wanted us caught?"

"Maybe he wants to watch us sweat."

"Robots don't sweat, Toshi."

"*A little.* Under lights." He sat down hard on the concrete floor with his back against the wall. "I don't know what he wants. I don't know what anyone wants. I used to fix torque curves in hip joints."

We sat there a while. Outside, a truck went by on the county road, and the orange door rattled in its track.

"We go," I said finally.

Toshi looked up.

"We go," I said again. "Because if we don't, it's over anyway. And because a man who meant us harm wouldn't have warned us. And because—" I stopped.

"Because what?"

I looked at Noah, sitting there with his hands folded and his eyes closed.

"Because I have a feeling," I said, "that we're not the only ones who need this to work."

\* \* \*

The address was a townhouse in Cincinnati, three stories of red brick on a quiet street full of trees older than the country. A brass plate by the door said PRIVATE PRACTICE, and nothing else. The black sedan dropped Noah at the curb at 9:00 a.m. sharp, and he climbed the steps with the easy, loose-shouldered confidence of a man who had never once in his life been kept waiting.

In a storage unit in Paperton, two hundred and fifty miles north, I sat in a green camping chair with a blanket over my knees and a bucket beside me, in case the nerves came out the wrong way.

"Heart rate's a hundred and twelve," Toshi said, from the next room of my mind. "Your real one."

"Stop telling me that."

"It's my job."

"It's making it worse."

"Okay." A pause. "It's a hundred and fifteen now."

\* \* \*

The waiting room was paneled in dark wood, with oil portraits of men in high collars who all seemed to have been painted in the same mood. There was one other person there, a woman in a nurse's scrubs sitting at a small desk with a clipboard. She didn't look like a nurse. She looked like someone who'd been told to sit in a room and watch the door, and who was very good at it.

"Mr. Fiatt," she said. "The doctor will be right with you."

Noah sat. I made him cross one leg over the other and look at his watch, because that's what important men do in waiting rooms. The watch said 9:04. I watched the second hand go around, and around, and I thought about all the drawings I'd done of clocks in my life, and how the hands always want to look like they're pointing somewhere.

At 9:09 an inner door opened.

I'd expected an old man. Some courtly society physician with a silver mustache, a pocket watch, a leather bag that had belonged to his grandfather. What came through the door was a woman in her forties, brisk and plain, in a white coat with her hair pulled back, carrying a tablet.

"Mr. Fiatt," she said. "I'm Dr. Veritas. Dr. Penrose is unwell this morning, so I'm covering. I hope that's all right."

The nurse at the desk looked up sharply. For just a second her face did something complicated. Then she looked down at her clipboard again.

"Of course," I said, in Noah's warm gravel voice.

As Dr. Veritas turned to lead us in, I caught a glimpse of the lanyard around her neck. It was tucked mostly inside her coat. But the clip was showing, and on the clip was a tiny logo I'd last seen on the Mindlink letter at my kitchen table, and on the wall of a clinic that used to be an Applebee's.

A little brain made of glowing dots, holding hands with itself.

"Toshi," I said silently. "Look at her lanyard."

There was a pause in my head.

"That's Mindlink," he said.

\* \* \*

The exam room was bright and white and very cold. Dr. Veritas had me sit on the paper-covered table and take off Noah's jacket and shirt, and I did it slowly, carefully, the way you undress in front of a stranger, and I felt more naked than I'd ever felt in my own body. Noah's chest was perfect. Smooth, tan, lightly haired, with a small scar on the left shoulder that Proxy had added, Toshi told me later, because a man without a single scar makes people nervous.

The nurse from the waiting room came in and stood by the door with her clipboard. Nobody had asked her to.

"Deep breath," said Dr. Veritas, and put the stethoscope on Noah's chest.

I made him breathe. In, out. In, out. Under the cold disc of the stethoscope there was nothing. No heart. Just the soft, steady whir of a coolant pump, turning like a ceiling fan in an empty house.

Dr. Veritas listened for a long time.

In Paperton, my real heart was going like a hammer on a tin roof. I could feel it through the connection. I could feel both at once, my racket and Noah's hush, and the gap between them was the most frightening sound I'd ever heard.

The nurse at the door leaned slightly forward.

Dr. Veritas moved the stethoscope an inch to the left. Listened again. Then she took it out of her ears, looped it around her neck, and made a note on her tablet.

"Strong heart," she said. "Very regular."

The nurse leaned back again.

I didn't breathe. Noah did, because I'd forgotten to tell him to stop.

\* \* \*

The EKG came next. Dr. Veritas stuck little white pads to Noah's chest and wrists and ankles, and clipped wires to them, and the wires ran to a small gray machine on a cart. Except I was watching, the way I'd learned to watch in thirty-one years of kids hiding phones under their desks, and I saw where the wires went. They didn't go to the machine. They went into the machine's side panel and came right back out again, bundled under the cart, to the tablet in her hand.

The screen on the cart lit up. A green line began to march across it. Up, down, spike, dip. Up, down, spike, dip. A perfect, healthy, middle-aged American heartbeat, beating for a man who had no heart at all.

"Beautiful," said Dr. Veritas, not looking at it.

Then she picked up the needle.

"Just a small pinch," she said.

Toshi said something in my head that I won't repeat.

She tied the rubber band around Noah's arm, swabbed the inside of his elbow with alcohol, and turned slightly on her stool, so that for just a moment her back was to the nurse at the door. It was a small movement. The kind a magician makes. If I hadn't spent three decades watching children try to palm erasers, I would never have seen it.

The needle went into the arm. I felt it the way you feel a pinch through a thick coat, far away and unimportant.

The vial on the end of the needle filled with blood.

Dark red. Real. Swirling.

I stared at it through Noah's eyes, and for one dizzy second I genuinely did not know what I was looking at. Then I saw it: the vial had been full before it touched him. There'd been a second one in her palm the whole time. The one that had actually gone into the arm was in her coat pocket now, and whatever was in it was blue and smelled like a new shower curtain.

She capped the full vial, labeled it, and handed it over her shoulder to the nurse without looking.

"For the lab," she said.

The nurse took it. She held it up to the light. She looked at it for a long moment.

Then she wrote something on her clipboard, and left the room.

\* \* \*

"You're in excellent health, Mr. Fiatt," said Dr. Veritas, pulling off the pads one by one. "Better than most men your age. Better than most men half your age." She peeled the last one from his ankle. "Keep doing whatever you're doing."

I put Noah's shirt back on. My fingers, his fingers, fumbled a little on the buttons. She noticed. She didn't say anything.

She walked me to the inner door. With her hand on the knob, she paused, and without turning her head, she spoke, very quietly, in the voice people use when they're talking to someone who isn't in the room.

"Mindlink sends its regards."

I said nothing. I wasn't sure Noah's mouth still worked.

"And tell him," she said, even more quietly, "that the headaches are dehydration. Most of our older participants don't drink enough water after the procedure. Eight glasses a day."

She opened the door.

"Have a wonderful day, Mr. Fiatt."

\* \* \*

The sedan brought Noah back to Paperton at two in the afternoon. By then I'd already let go, somewhere around Dayton, because my hands had started shaking so badly Toshi was afraid it would bleed through the connection. I sat in the camping chair with the blanket around my shoulders and drank a whole bottle of water in one long pull, and then I started laughing, and then I stopped.

"They know," Toshi said. He hadn't sat down since nine. "Mindlink knows. They know it's you. They know about the implant. They know about the robot. They sent their own doctor, Harold. They got rid of the real one."

"I know."

"They could have ended us in that room. One word to that nurse. One." He turned in a tight circle. "Why didn't they?"

I looked across at Noah in his chair, eyes closed, hands folded. Somewhere inside him was a line of code nobody could read, and somewhere inside me was a chip made by a company whose partners owned every thought I'd had since March.

I thought about page thirty-eight of the consent form. *Mindlink Labs and its partners.* I thought about how Toshi's cable had plugged into Noah so easily, *almost like somebody designed them to fit together*.

I thought about a vial of blue coolant, sitting in the pocket of a Mindlink doctor's coat, that could bring down a great deal more than one old man in Paperton.

"Because they can't," I said.

Toshi stopped circling.

"If they expose Noah," I said, working it out as I went, "somebody asks what Noah is. And then somebody asks who else is one. And whatever Mindlink's part in that is, it goes on the front page too." I set the empty bottle down on the concrete. "We're not the only ones hiding something in this room, Toshi. We're just the only ones who didn't know it."

The storage unit was quiet. Outside, the Dollar Depot sign buzzed. DOLL R DEP.

After a while, Toshi went to the cooler and got me another bottle of water. He set it down next to my chair without a word.

I drank it. Eight glasses a day. Doctor's orders.

---

items.title: I finally visited Pubkey in Washington DC
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/162019)

I am attending a reunion of sorts of some old friends in DC.  I had some free time yesterday, so I finally got the opportunity to visit the Washington Pubkey.

I have posted a few times about the NYC version. I have a great time whenever I go:

https://stacker.news/items/219987/r/siggy47

https://stacker.news/items/230440/r/siggy47

https://stacker.news/items/1283387/r/siggy47

The Washington DC version of Pubkey is located on 7th Street in the [Penn Quarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Quarter) neighborhood of the city. It's not far from Ford's Theater and the J Edgar Hoover FBI building.  Capital One Arena, where the Washington Capitals play, is down the block. It is an upscale, touristy location.

Pubkey DC opened in January, 2026, according to the website, but I thought it had been around longer.  Yesterday the Washington Capitals had an early game, so there were plenty of fans in jerseys milling about. When I walked in I immediately noticed how different this place was from the New York version. It's huge, around 12,000 square feet, with two bars, a stage, and big screens everywhere showing sporting events. There was a good crowd, which looked to be a mix of tourists, locals, and hockey fans. I can't be certain, but I'm pretty sure I was the only person in the place interested in bitcoin.

This is not an in your face bitcoin space. I had just had a long car and was hungry. I decided to sit at the bar and have some lunch after exploring a bit.

At first I didn't notice much bitcoin stuff, but it is all strategically placed to fit in unobtrusively. I liked the low key design. It could be any sports /tourist spot in any city.

There were a few stickers in the men's room:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162028)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162029)

I then noticed a large wall display with some actively mining bitaxes:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162030)

And this small, but intriguing stack of bitcoin and bitcoin adjacent books below a "Free Samourai" sign:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162032)

I sat at the bar and saw this cool display:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162033)

Occasionally the ticker had a news flash scrolling across the screen.

When ordering my lunch I let the bartender know that I planned to pay in bitcoin. I was told that if I did, I would receive a 21% discount, which is impressive. I asked about the payment setup, and was a little disappointed that they just use square. I tried to.engage my server in a little bitcoin banter, but it was obvious he had no deep interest. I dont want to sound negative. All of the workers were friendly and competent. The menu was similar to the NYC Pubkey. I had a Caesar wrap, which was very good.  I must say paying with the square app was quick and easy. You select the tip amount before the invoice is generated, which is nice. I have experienced a few awkward moments trying to tip at the NYC Pubkey. You never can be sure if the server would prefer sats or dollars. This way they probably get a choice.

That being said, paying with square is still disappointing.

On the way out I found this board near the front bar:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162036)

I guess this proves there are some bitcoiners patronizing the place.

I didn't get to experience an event, but there is plenty of room for bitcoin gatherings. NYC Pubkey always feels a little cramped. I know Thomas Massie will be holding a discussion soon. I hope I get some time on my next trip to catch a presentation.

items.text:
> **Escaping Venezuela lays bare the human cost of the socialist project.**
>
> The documentary [Escaping Venezuela](https://escapingvenezuela.reason.com/) portrays the unprecedented unfolding of the contemporary Venezuelan crisis, one that cannot be grasped through constitutional, political science, international law, or electoral analysis alone. Its present dimensions are rooted in a broader historical arc spanning 1958 to 2026. That arc began with a functioning, peaceful yet imperfect democracy in what was then one of Latin America’s wealthiest nations (1958–1999). It gave way to twenty-first-century socialism under Hugo Chávez (1999–2013) and Nicolás Maduro (2013–2026), an era defined by institutional decay, the dismantling of democracy, the capture of state institutions by criminal networks with international ties, profound economic and social collapse, and systematic human rights violations. It now enters a new phase marked by the Trump administration’s asserted control over Venezuela, following the January 3, 2026, military operation that seized Nicolás Maduro, whom much of the international community regarded as a usurper, and brought him before the United States (U.S.) federal courts. 
>
> At the beginning of Venezuela’s democratic era, the system relied on consensus among the major political parties on key issues. It also gradually incorporated national business organizations, labor unions, and religious groups into a semi-corporatist framework that allowed them to participate in key economic and political decisions. Over time, the bipartisan system evolved into a complex, conflict-ridden multiparty system, with organizations outside the parties becoming increasingly influential. This convergence of diverse, competing interests, along with the risk these groups perceived to their sometimes-opaque privileges and interests from the market-friendly economic reforms of the late 1980s, weakened democracy and enabled practices that undermined economic and political integrity.  
>
> The documentary vividly describes how during the second presidency of social democrat Carlos Andrés Pérez (1989–1993), Venezuela was shaken by the *Caracazo,* a wave of protests, riots, and looting that began on February 27, 1989. Amnesty International reported that human rights organizations identified approximately 400 people who died or went missing during the events. Some commentators contend that the *Caracazo* was planned rather than entirely spontaneous. They cite reports that politically active students occupied public transportation facilities at 6 a.m. on February 27, 1989, and distributed preprinted leaflets. They also point to allegations that police had been instructed not to intervene, while President Carlos Andrés Pérez blamed police insubordination. Some accounts cite evidence of coordination and identify Jorge Rodríguez, then a student leader and later a prominent figure in Venezuela’s socialist government, as an organizer. Paulina Gamus, who chaired the congressional inquiry, believed the unrest had been orchestrated but had spiraled out of control. Chávez later said the *Caracazo* helped spur his plans for the 1992 coup attempt.
>
> [**...read more at civitasoutlook.com**](https://www.civitasoutlook.com/research/the-fall-of-venezuela-29f77b11-3ad0-49e3-abfb-4e53db499870)

items.title: Forgotten Internet Tech?
items.text:
Lately I have been spending a lot of time exploring old software and technologies on my Linux netbook. Working on SkyLordsLab BBS made me realize how many interesting things from the early internet have been forgotten.

We have modern applications for almost everything now. But I wonder how many old ideas were actually good and simply got left behind.

So here is my question.

What is one forgotten internet technology or old piece of software that you think deserves a second chance?

It could be an old protocol. A forgotten application. A strange communication system. Or something most people have never even heard of.

I am looking for something unusual to explore. Maybe I will even try bringing one of those ideas back to life on my old antiX netbook

items.title: Blok’s Stack Strategy: How I use LN Markets to trade  daily to stack moar sats
items.text:
## Disclaimer:

#### Don’t be a degen and waste sats like me. 

BUT!!

If you have an appetite for risk and want to grow your stack you can trade on LN Markets.

I do this for the reasons below.

1. The LN Markets team has built a tremendous trading platform only using lightning. I want to support the platform and use lightning every day (why I am addicted to SN) 

2. As the price rises you can stack moar sats with the sat stash you have. Plus you know your sat stack is increasing with every price pump. So not only are you feeling richer in fiat terms but also in sat terms 

3. As the price falls you can catch a falling knife and play the “when is the bottom in”

4. I am not risk adverse. I trade on sats I can afford to lose. I zapped and spent way more sats on SN than I have traded on LN markets

5. It takes the edge off on FOMO. 

## The Strategy:

It’s quite simple I enter a trade every day.  With the following parameters 

1. I do a modest position size. 

* If I feel bearish I do $15 
* If I feel bullish I do $150 to $200

2. Then I set it to 10x leverage 

3. Then I set the take profits at 25% and the stop loss at 8% 

4. I market buy

I let the trades run for as long as possible. Once the price moves up I move the stop losses up accordingly to preserve capital. 

If we get a massive pump before my take profits get triggered I let the trade just run 


![](https://m.stacker.news/125936)

`I never do puts or shorts! I AM FORVER LONG PERMABULL`


## Progres to date 

I only got 22 running trades. I had a lot more open but when the bitcoin price dips my stop losses hit.

items.title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
items.text:
> **Moritz Hardt, author of a new book on benchmarks, believes these “standardized tests” for artificial intelligence are fundamentally broken — but not unfixable.**
>
> Benchmarks are the rulers of AI, in both senses of the word. As measuring sticks, they work according to an extremely simple logic: If you want to know what an AI model can do, devise a standardized test to gauge it. But AI benchmarks can also dominate the behavior of the entire field.
>
> In 1987, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s [first benchmark](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.06647v1#S5) on automatic speech-to-text translation showed that state-of-the-art AI could not outperform so-called “dumb” statistical approaches. The poor performance helped to usher in an AI winter. For 25 years, interest in AI research waned and funding dried up.
>
> Then, in 2012, [another benchmark](https://www.image-net.org/challenges/LSVRC/index.php) called ImageNet swung the pendulum back. An eight-layer neural network [trounced](https://spectrum.ieee.org/alexnet-source-code) other algorithms at classifying images and kicked off a “deep learning revolution.”
>
> Nowadays, new AI benchmarks, geared at large language models such as OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, get created and solved with clockwork regularity, purporting to measure everything from [domain-specific expertise](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report/technical-performance) to “[general intelligence](https://arcprize.org/arc-agi).” But rather than hail this trend as proof of AI’s skyrocketing potential, many in the field — [skeptics](https://x.com/GaryMarcus/status/2028488127875342724) and [boosters](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1896266683301659068?lang=en) alike — take it as evidence that benchmarking itself has become [fatally flawed](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-02462-5).
>
> [**...read more at quantamagazine.org**](https://www.quantamagazine.org/he-wants-ai-benchmarking-to-be-a-science-not-a-dark-art-20261016/)
